questions.stem: What did the model do when it returned jelly? A brand manager types 'Peanut butter and' into a chat model and it returns 'jelly'. She wants to know what the model did, so that she can judge what else to trust it with.
options: It worked out which single word most often follows the text it was given
It searched the web for the phrase and copied the most popular ending
It applied a grammar rule that requires a noun after the word and
It looked the phrase up in a stored table of common English sayings
why: ✓ a language model is trained to predict the next token. Given 'Peanut butter and', it scores every possible next token from the patterns of its training text, and jelly scores far above the rest.
✗ a chat model without a search tool writes from what it learned in training; it did not visit the web for this phrase.
✗ the model holds no rulebook of grammar. It learned patterns from text, and many nouns could follow 'and'.
✗ there is no stored table of sayings to look up; the model stores weights learned from text, and the next token comes from those.
questions.explanation: The model did next-token prediction: it scored every possible next token from patterns in its training text and 'jelly' scored highest. Nothing was searched, looked up or checked. So the manager can trust it with text that follows common patterns, but should check anything that has to be true.
questions.trap: B ('It searched the web for the phrase and copied the most popular ending'). It sounds modern, because some chat products can search. But this model had no search tool: it wrote the next token from patterns it learned in training.
questions.tip: Next-token questions: pick the option that says the model scored or predicted the next token from training patterns. Reject anything that says it searched, looked up or applied a rule.
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 1 Part 1 (PDF), pp. 39-42 and 50-59: trained to predict the next token; Peanut butter and -> jelly. LECTURE Week 3 Lecture, slides 6 and 7: a base model is finishing your paragraph. LECTURE Week 1 Part 1 (PDF), pp. 75-81: Four score and seven, one token at a time until a stopping condition. READING Bonus Technical Lecture Notes, slide 21.

questions.official: Quiz 1 · Q2 — Predictive and generative AI
questions.stem: Which proposal is predictive and which is generative? A finance team is shown two proposals. The first scores every open invoice and flags the ones likely to be paid late. The second drafts the reminder letter that goes to those customers. The controller asks which is predictive work and which is generative work.
options: The first is predictive and the second is generative
Both are generative, because both use a trained model
The first is generative and the second is predictive
Both are predictive, because both were trained on past invoices
why: ✓ predictive AI takes a case and returns a score or label learned from past cases with known outcomes (is this invoice likely to be paid late?); generative AI takes a prompt and returns new content (a letter written one token at a time).
✗ both use trained models, but the first returns a score for each invoice, which is prediction.
✗ this swaps them: scoring invoices is prediction, and writing a new letter is generation.
✗ training on past invoices does not make the letter predictive; the second proposal produces new text.
questions.explanation: Scoring invoices for late payment is predictive AI (a score or label learned from past cases with known outcomes). Drafting the reminder letter is generative AI (new content from a prompt). Both use trained models, so what decides the label is what comes out: a score, or new text.
questions.trap: B ('Both are generative, because both use a trained model'). It is true that both use trained models, so it sounds safe. But the label comes from what comes out: a score or label (predictive) or new content (generative).
questions.tip: Ask 'what comes out?' A score or label learned from past cases = predictive. New text, code or images = generative. Acts in other systems through tools in a loop = agentic.
questions.source: Where we met it: AIS Week 2 AIS, slide 5: definitions of predictive, generative and agentic AI. LECTURE Week 1 Part 1 (PDF), pp. 36-37: the machine learning pipeline and the spam filter. AIS Week 2 AIS, slide 6: the same task under each paradigm. READING Bonus Technical Lecture Notes, slide 16: a cancellation score against a retention message.

questions.stem: Why did the model say 9.11 is larger than 9.9? A junior accountant asks a chat model which write-off is larger, 9.11 or 9.9. The model answers 9.11 and explains itself fluently. The figure shows what the model received: 'You type 9.11' -> 3 pieces [9][.][11]; 'You type 9.9' -> 3 pieces [9][.][9]. 'The part after the point arrives as 11 against 9. Read as whole numbers, 11 is the larger one. Nothing in the sentence tells the model these are decimal places.'
options: The model has a rounding error in its arithmetic module
The model treated both values as text and compared 11 against 9
The model was trained mostly on software version numbers
The model needed the currency stated before it could compare
why: ✗ the model has no arithmetic module to round with; the error comes from the pieces the numbers arrive in.
✓ a model reads tokens. 9.11 arrives as 9, the point and 11, and 9.9 as 9, the point and 9. Read as whole numbers, 11 is larger than 9, and nothing tells the model these are decimal places.
✗ nothing in the figure points to version numbers; it shows the three pieces each value became, and those explain the answer.
✗ a currency sign would not help, because the digits after the point would still arrive as separate pieces.
questions.explanation: A model reads tokens (pieces of text), not numbers. 9.11 becomes 9 / . / 11 and 9.9 becomes 9 / . / 9, so it compares 11 against 9 and gives a fluent wrong answer. The work fix: for any comparison or sum, ask the model to write and run code, and check the code.
questions.trap: A ('The model has a rounding error in its arithmetic module'). 'Rounding error' sounds technical and plausible. But a language model has no arithmetic module: it reads 9.11 and 9.9 as pieces of text (tokens) and compares 11 with 9.
questions.tip: Numbers in a prompt = tokens (pieces of text). Any option about an 'arithmetic module' is wrong. The fix is always: ask it to write and run code, then check the code.
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 1 whiteboard 3 on eLearn: 9.9 against 9.22, boxed as tokens. LECTURE Week 1 Part 1 (PDF), pp. 44-46: tokens are not words. PROBLEM SET Problem Set 2, panel 13: the numbers on your screen are text. QUIZ Review Quiz, Weeks 1 to 3, item 5.

questions.official: Quiz 1 · Q4 — The spread of next tokens
questions.stem: Has the model settled on 'alike' as the next word? The figure shows what the model is holding after the words 'All happy families are' (bar chart, 'probability of being the next piece of text': alike 0.27, different 0.11, joyful 0.06, unique 0.04, the same 0.03, happy 0.02; caption 'The model holds a spread of candidates, not one answer. Decoding is what picks from it.'). A colleague concludes from it that the model knows the answer is alike.
options: Wrong, because the numbers shown are relevance scores and not chances
Correct, because a candidate above 0.25 is treated as settled
Correct, because the model stores the quotation and recalls it
Wrong, because the figure shows a spread and something else still picks
why: ✗ the axis says what the numbers are: the probability of being the next piece of text.
✗ no threshold of 0.25 settles an answer; the decoding rule does the picking, whatever the top value is.
✗ the model does not store the quotation and recall it; it gives every candidate a chance, and alike is one of them.
✓ the model holds a probability for each candidate (alike 0.27, different 0.11, joyful 0.06...). Alike is the most likely but 0.27 is far from certain; a separate step, decoding, then picks one.
questions.explanation: The colleague is wrong: the model holds a spread of probabilities, and 0.27 for 'alike' is only about a one-in-four chance. A separate step, decoding, does the picking, and how it picks is a setting you control: greedy decoding takes 'alike' every time, while sampling can return 'different' or 'joyful'.
questions.trap: C ('Correct, because the model stores the quotation and recalls it'). The Tolstoy line is famous, so 'it stores the quotation' feels true. But the model stores weights, not quotes; it holds a spread of probabilities and a separate step (decoding) picks.
questions.tip: If a figure shows a bar chart of probabilities, the answer is 'a spread, and decoding picks'. 0.27 is about a one-in-four chance, not 'known'.
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 1 Part 1 (PDF), pp. 50-58: alike at 27%; greedy decoding takes the top token. LECTURE Week 1 Part 1 (PDF), pp. 59-72: sampling is rolling a weighted die. AIS Week 1 AIS, slide 8, and Week 2 AIS, slide 22: output is non-deterministic, so your screens will not match. READING Bonus Technical Lecture Notes, slides 27-31.

questions.stem: How should temperature be set for a filing and for taglines? Two jobs run on the same model. One rewrites approved disclosure text for a filing, where the wording must come out the same every run. The other brainstorms campaign taglines, where sameness is the problem. The figure shows what the setting does ('Temperature does not change what the model knows. It changes how boldly it picks.' Three panels: Temperature 0 = one bar at 1.0 for alike; Temperature 1.0 = the learned spread; Temperature 1.6 = flatter spread; 'same model, same prompt, same candidates: only the picking changes').
options: Set both to zero, since reliable output is always preferable
Leave both at the default, since the setting affects only speed
Raise temperature for the filing and lower it for the taglines
Lower temperature for the filing and raise it for the taglines
why: ✗ zero suits the filing, but it would return the same tagline every run, which is the problem the brainstorm has.
✗ temperature does not set speed; it sets how tokens are picked, so the default is a choice like any other.
✗ this swaps the two jobs: a high temperature would vary the filing, and a low one would repeat the taglines.

✓ at 0 the model takes the top token every time, so approved disclosure wording comes out the same each run; a higher temperature flattens the spread, so less likely tokens appear and the taglines vary.
questions.explanation: The filing needs a low temperature and the taglines a higher one. Temperature changes how boldly the model picks from the same spread: at 0 it always takes the top token (repeatable), and higher values flatten the spread (more variety). The model and its candidates stay the same; only the picking changes.
questions.trap: A ('Set both to zero, since reliable output is always preferable'). 'Reliable output is always better' sounds sensible. But at temperature 0 the taglines would come out the same every run, which is exactly the brainstorm's problem.
questions.tip: Temperature = how boldly the model picks. Must-repeat text: low (near 0). Variety: raise it moderately. It never makes an answer more correct.
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 1 Part 1 (PDF), p. 68: temperature and randomness. NOTEBOOK AI+Py Day, Local LLMs as Your Database, Lesson 2: temperature 0 with seed 6110. NOTEBOOK AI+Py Day, Weeks 4 to 5 (27 September), Probe 3: the same question at 0.0 and at 0.8. READING Bonus Technical Lecture Notes, slides 32 and 33: why run again gives a new tagline.

questions.official: Quiz 1 · Q10 — What these systems do
questions.stem: At a family dinner: which claim is not true? At a family dinner, four claims about these systems come up. As an MBAI student you are asked which one is NOT true (misinformation about AI).
options: It can give two different answers to the same question
It can produce a confident answer that is not grounded in fact
It looks up each answer in a database of verified facts
It knows nothing about events after its training finished
why: ✗ with sampling at a temperature above 0, the same question can get different answers.
✗ it is the made-up answer of Questions 8 and 9.
✓ a language model writes each answer from patterns learned in training, one token at a time, and checks nothing against a database.
✗ what the model learned stops at its training cut-off, unless a tool such as search adds newer text to its context.
questions.explanation: The false claim is that it looks up each answer in a database of verified facts: a model writes from patterns learned in training, one token at a time, and checks nothing. The other three are true: sampling can vary answers, fluent answers can lack grounding, and it knows nothing after its training cut-off unless a tool such as web search adds it. As the AI+Py Day notebook put it: 'the database is your documents, and the model is the reader.'
questions.trap: D ('It knows nothing about events after its training finished'). Many people know chat products can search, so 'knows nothing after training' looks false. It is true: without a tool such as search, the model's knowledge stops at its cut-off.
questions.tip: NOT questions: mark each option True or False first, then pick the single False. The false claim here is 'looks up verified facts' - a model checks nothing.
questions.source: Where we met it: NOTEBOOK AI+Py Day, Local LLMs as Your Database, What to take away: the database is your documents, and the model is the reader. LECTURE Week 1 Part 1 (PDF), pp. 71, 72 and 82-84: several outputs for the same input; pre-trained. LECTURE Week 3 Lecture, slide 8: all the knowledge arrived during pre-training. QUIZ Review Quiz, Weeks 1 to 3, item 22.

questions.official: Quiz 2 · Q4 — Greedy and sampled decoding
questions.stem: Why is greedy deterministic and sampling stochastic? Figure 1 shows the full distribution in a simplified five-token vocabulary. Which statement correctly describes why greedy decoding is 'deterministic', whereas sampling is 'stochastic'? (Figure 1. After 'All happy families are', over five tokens: alike 0.40, different 0.25, joyful 0.17, unique 0.12, zooming 0.06; the five add to 1.00. Values other than 0.40 are illustrative.)
options: Greedy decoding chooses every token with equal probability.
Greedy decoding chooses "alike"; sampling can choose another token.
A probability of 0.40 means "alike" occurred in exactly 40% of training sentences.
Sampling must choose "alike" because it has the highest probability.
why: ✗ equal chances describe a fair die. Greedy is the opposite and always takes the top token.

✓ greedy decoding takes the most likely token, so it writes alike on every run ('taking its mode'); sampling rolls the weighted die, so alike comes up about 40% of the time and the others in proportion to their chances.
✗ these are probabilities the model learned in training, not counts of sentences; it scores sequences it never read.
✗ sampling can pick a less likely token. Always taking the highest is the definition of greedy.
questions.explanation: Greedy decoding always takes the top token ('alike', 0.40), so it gives the same output every run (deterministic). Sampling draws from the spread like a weighted die, so 'alike' comes up about 40% of the time and other tokens in proportion to their chances (stochastic).
questions.trap: D ('Sampling must choose "alike" because it has the highest probability'). 'Highest probability wins' sounds natural. But always taking the top token is the definition of greedy; sampling can pick a less likely token.
questions.tip: Greedy = take the mode = same output every run (deterministic). Sampling = roll a weighted die = runs differ (stochastic).
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 1 Part 1 (PDF), pp. 54-60: the distribution; greedy takes the mode, or we sample. LECTURE Week 1 Part 1 (PDF), pp. 61-67: sampling is rolling a weighted die. NOTEBOOK AI+Py Day, Weeks 4 to 5 (27 September), Probe 3: at temperature 0 the seed did nothing. READING Bonus Technical Lecture Notes, slides 29-31, for revision.

questions.stem: How do we get varied headlines from the same prompt? A marketing team wants varied headline candidates from the same model and prompt. It currently uses a very low sampling temperature. Which change most directly addresses the lack of variety?
options: Increase temperature and publish every result because variation establishes quality.
Increase temperature moderately, then review the candidates for suitability and accuracy.
Reduce temperature further to make less likely word choices more common.
Keep temperature fixed and assume identical outputs prove the best headline was found.
why: ✗ variation does not establish quality, and publishing without review skips the judging step.
✓ raising temperature flattens the spread so less likely words appear and candidates vary; a person still judges every candidate; 'moderately' because above 1 the output can turn chaotic.
✗ this runs the wrong way: lowering temperature makes the likely words more dominant still.
✗ identical outputs show the setting at work. A temperature near 0 makes an answer repeatable, which says nothing about whether it is best.
questions.explanation: Raise temperature moderately, then review the candidates. At a very low temperature the model takes the most likely token almost every time, so headlines barely change; raising it flattens the spread so they vary. Variety is not quality and temperature never makes the model better informed, so a person still judges every candidate; above 1 output can turn chaotic, hence 'moderately'.
questions.trap: A ('Increase temperature and publish every result because variation establishes quality'). It contains the right first move (raise temperature). But 'publish every result' skips the human review, and variety is not quality.
questions.tip: Look for 'moderately' + 'review'. More temperature = more variety, never more correctness; a person still judges.
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 1 Part 1 (PDF), p. 68: above 1, creative but possibly chaotic output. QUIZ Review Quiz, Weeks 1 to 3, items 15 and 20: variety at the cost of predictability. NOTEBOOK AI+Py Day, Weeks 4 to 5 (27 September), Probe 3: ask it twice. READING Bonus Technical Lecture Notes, slides 32 and 33, for revision.

questions.stem: A multinational subscription business wants to reduce customer churn. Its marketing team uses the system in the figure below. Which description best fits this use of AI? (Figure: customer data -> a cancellation risk for each customer -> a marketer reviews and chooses actions; scores every Monday, from several countries.)
options: It is predictive AI because predictive systems always operate without human decisions.
It is agentic AI because the model uses data from several countries.
It is agentic AI because the report is produced automatically every Monday.
It is predictive AI because it estimates which customers are likely to leave; the marketing team decides what action to take.
why: ✗ 'The label is right and the reason is wrong. Predictive systems do not always run without people; here a marketer decides.'
✗ 'Where the data comes from has nothing to do with being agentic, which needs a goal, tools, a loop and a stop.'
✗ 'An automatic Monday report is a trigger and fixed steps, like the Monday campaign report of Week 7, which was a fixed workflow.'
✓ 'It is predictive AI: it estimates which customers are likely to leave, and the marketing team decides what to do.'
questions.explanation: Predictive AI takes a case in and gives a score or label out, learned from past cases with known outcomes - like a bank's model for loan applications. The churn model gives each customer a risk of cancelling; it chooses no tools, runs no loop and takes no action, and a marketer reads the scores and chooses retention actions. Running every Monday, or using data from several countries, changes neither point.
questions.trap: C ('It is agentic AI because the report is produced automatically every Monday'). A report that appears automatically every Monday feels 'agentic'. But a schedule plus fixed steps is a workflow; the model only returns a score.
questions.tip: Score or label out, a person decides = predictive AI. Agentic needs a goal, tools, a loop and a stop. Check the REASON in the option, not only the label (option A has the right label, wrong reason).
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 9 Lecture, slide 13 (a model that returns a label with a probability; the automation that calls it does the acting); LECTURE Week 1 Part 1 (PDF), pp. 36 and 37 (from training to foresight, the predictive pipeline); Week 7 Map deck, slide 4 (AI scores a claim, and the adjuster decides the payout); READING Week 10 Lecture, slides 10, 11 and 16, for revision (a case in, a label out; a person who signs).

questions.stem: Define a token. An analyst pastes a column of 40 expense amounts, such as 1,240.50 and 98.75, into a chat model and asks for the total. The model returns a fluent figure. Explain why the figure may be wrong, and say what the analyst should do instead.

parts.label: (a)
parts.task: Define a token.
parts.model: A token is a piece of text, about three-quarters of an English word on average. The model reads and writes tokens, and a number such as 1,240.50 can arrive as several pieces.

parts.label: (b)
parts.task: Explain why the fluent total may be wrong.
parts.model: The model writes the most likely next tokens and runs no arithmetic, so a total built from the pieces of 40 numbers can read well and be wrong, as 9.11 against 9.9 was in Quiz 1.

parts.label: (c)
parts.task: Apply it to the 40-line case.
parts.model: Each of the 40 lines is another chance of a slip, and nothing in a fluent reply marks one. The analyst asks the model to write and run code that sums the column, or sums it in a spreadsheet.

parts.label: (d)
parts.task: Say what the analyst should check or do.
parts.model: The analyst reads the code, compares its result with a spreadsheet total or a control total from the source system, and records which file was summed.

questions.modelAnswer: (a) A token is a piece of text, about three-quarters of an English word on average. The model reads and writes tokens, and a number such as 1,240.50 can arrive as several pieces. (b) The model writes the most likely next tokens and runs no arithmetic, so a total built from the pieces of 40 numbers can read well and be wrong, as 9.11 against 9.9 was in Quiz 1. (c) Each of the 40 lines is another chance of a slip, and nothing in a fluent reply marks one. The analyst asks the model to write and run code that sums the column, or sums it in a spreadsheet. (d) The analyst reads the code, compares its result with a spreadsheet total or a control total from the source system, and records which file was summed.
questions.explanation: Define: a token as a piece of text the model reads and writes, noting a number can split into several tokens. Explain: the model predicts the next tokens and runs no arithmetic, so a fluent total can be wrong. Apply: name the risk across 40 lines and the fix, which is code that sums the column, or a spreadsheet. Check: compare the result with a control total and record which file was summed.
questions.trap: Saying the model made an arithmetic error. It does no arithmetic; it predicts tokens.
questions.tip: A full answer does all four parts; an answer that only defines earns one point (p.4, p.152).
questions.source: Where we met it: Lecture: Week 1 Part 1 (PDF), pp. 44 to 46: tokens are not words; Problem Set 2, panel 13: the numbers on your screen are text; Quiz 1, Question 3

questions.stem: Your analysts write the answers: which step is this? Your firm licenses a base model that continues text instead of answering. You hire ten experienced analysts and ask each to write out, in full, the answer they would give to a list of typical client requests. You then train the model on those written answers. Which step have you run? (Figure: 'The three-step repair applied on top of GPT-3': Step 1 Show it what an answer looks like / People WRITE the answers / about 13,000 prompts; Step 2 Build a judge out of rankings / People RANK the answers / about 33,000 questions; Step 3 Let the judge do the teaching / People do NOTHING / about 31,000 questions.)
options: Step 2, because experienced people were the ones producing the material
Step 3, because the model is being adjusted by a training signal
None of them, because this is retrieval and not training at all
Step 1, because people wrote the answers the model learns to imitate
why: ✗ Step 2 asks people to rank answers the model wrote; who the people are does not decide the step.
✗ in Step 3 the training signal is a judge's score; here the signal is the written answers themselves.
✗ the model is trained on the answers, so its weights change. Retrieval would leave the model as it was and fetch text at question time.
✓ Step 1, supervised fine-tuning, shows a base model what an answer looks like: people write full answers to typical requests and the model is trained to imitate them.
questions.explanation: This is Step 1, supervised fine-tuning (SFT): people WRITE full answers and the base model is trained to imitate them. The analysts' experience matters for answer quality, but what makes it Step 1 is that people wrote the answers. In the InstructGPT study behind the figure, this step used about 13,000 prompts.
questions.trap: A ('Step 2, because experienced people were the ones producing the material'). Experienced people producing material sounds like the 'expert judge' step. But what decides the step is what people do: they WRITE answers here, which is Step 1.
questions.tip: Remember by verbs: Step 1 people WRITE (supervised fine-tuning), Step 2 people RANK (reward model), Step 3 people do NOTHING (the judge teaches).
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 1 Part 2 (PDF), pp. 9-15: Step 1, supervised fine-tuning. LECTURE Week 3 Lecture, slides 8 and 9: show it what an answer looks like. LECTURE Week 3 whiteboard 2 on eLearn: 11,000 and 1,500 written pairs. READING Week 3 Bonus, slide 4: what fine-tuning changes, and when retrieval is the tool.

questions.official: Quiz 1 · Q7 — Step 2: the reward model
questions.stem: Your analysts rank the answers: what have you built? A year on, writing answers has become too slow. Instead you show each analyst several answers the model produced for the same request and ask them only to put those answers in order, best to worst. You then train a second model to reproduce that ordering. What have you built? (Same three-step figure as Q6.)
options: A larger version of the first model, trained on more material
A filter that blocks answers falling below a fixed quality score
A stand-in judge that scores answers the way your analysts did
A search index that finds the closest previously approved answer
why: ✗ the second model is a separate judge that scores answers and writes none, and it is smaller than the first.
✗ a filter with a fixed cut-off is a rule a person sets; the reward model learns graded scores from the rankings.
✓ this is Step 2. A second model trained to reproduce the ranking becomes a reward model: for any new answer it returns a score that predicts how your analysts would have ranked it.
✗ a search index returns stored answers, while the reward model scores any answer, including new ones nobody has seen.
questions.explanation: You have built a reward model, a stand-in judge (Step 2). Ranking answers is quicker than writing them, and the second model learns to predict the ranking, so it can score any new answer. In Step 3 that judge teaches the first model and no person reads each answer; Steps 2 and 3 together are called RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback).
questions.trap: B ('A filter that blocks answers falling below a fixed quality score'). A 'quality filter' sounds like what a judge does. But a fixed cut-off is a rule a person sets; the reward model learns graded scores from the rankings and can score any new answer.
questions.tip: Rankings in, a second model that scores answers out = the reward model, a stand-in judge (Step 2). Steps 2 + 3 together = RLHF.
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 1 Part 2 (PDF), pp. 16-24: ranking answers; the reward model scores 0.02 and 0.95. LECTURE Week 3 Lecture, slides 10 and 12: build a judge out of rankings. LECTURE Week 3 whiteboard 2 on eLearn: the ratings 0.02 and 0.95. LECTURE Week 1 Part 2 (PDF), p. 34: Steps 2 and 3 are called RLHF.

questions.stem: Three well-formatted studies, and none of them exists. A marketing manager asks a model for the three most cited independent studies on a niche product category. It returns three titles with authors and years, all formatted properly. None of the three exists. The figure shows the shape of the problem ('Confidence stays flat while reliability falls away': x-axis how much the training text covered this particular question; a flat line for how confident it sounds, a falling line for how often the answer is right; 'fabrication lives here' where coverage is thin).
options: The model produced plausible text where it had little to go on
The model misread the question and answered a different one
The model was working from an out-of-date copy of the literature
The model would have been right had the temperature been zero
why: ✓ this is a hallucination, a confident fabrication. A model writes the most plausible next tokens, and a well-formatted citation is plausible text; for a niche category the training text holds few real studies, so it fills the pattern.
✗ it answered the question it was asked, three studies with authors and years. The trouble is that the studies do not exist.
✗ an out-of-date copy would return real but older studies; these were never published at all.
✗ a temperature of 0 makes an answer repeatable, and it would repeat the same made-up titles.
questions.explanation: The model produced plausible text where it had little to go on: a hallucination, 'a confident fabrication rather than an error in the ordinary sense'. Because a citation with authors, year and journal is plausible text, the model can produce it for a study that does not exist. The figure shows confidence stays flat while how often it is right falls away where training coverage is thin.
questions.trap: D ('The model would have been right had the temperature been zero'). Temperature 0 sounds like 'more careful'. But it only makes the answer repeatable, so it would repeat the same made-up titles every time.
questions.tip: Made-up but well-formatted answer = plausible text where the training text had little to go on (a hallucination). Temperature does not fix it; opening the source does.
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 3 Lecture, slides 19 and 32: confident, complete and wrong. AIS Week 3 AIS, slides 6 and 17: an agent asked to guess will invent something reasonable. NOTEBOOK AI+Py Day, Local LLMs as Your Database, Lesson 7: 30 days, six times; the handbook says 60. PROBLEM SET Problem Set 2, panel 8: did it hand you something that looked right and was not?

questions.stem: Which questions need the most care? Having been caught once, the same manager wants to know which questions to be most careful with in future, so she can decide what to check and what to accept.
options: Questions about topics the training text is unlikely to have covered
Questions phrased as a request rather than as a direct question
Questions asked in the afternoon, when the service is under heavier load
Questions with long answers, since more text means more room for error
why: ✓ made-up answers gather in the silences, the places the training text barely covered: niche categories, recent events, local detail and private records such as her own firm's figures.
✗ phrasing a request as a question does not change what the training text covered.
✗ heavy load can slow a reply; it does not make the model invent studies.
✗ long answers give more room for slips, but a short answer on a thinly covered topic is the larger risk, as Question 8 showed.
questions.explanation: Take most care with topics the training text is unlikely to have covered: niche, recent, local and private (e.g. your own firm's records). On widely published facts the model is usually right. So she checks every niche, recent, local or private claim against a source she opens herself, and spends less checking on what is widely published.
questions.trap: D ('Questions with long answers, since more text means more room for error'). Long answers do give more room for slips, so this feels right. But the bigger risk is a short answer on a topic the training text barely covered.
questions.tip: Check most: niche, recent, local and private (your firm's own records). Widely published facts are usually right.
questions.source: Where we met it: QUIZ Review Quiz, Weeks 1 to 3, item 21: made-up answers gather where the training text is silent. NOTEBOOK AI+Py Day, Local LLMs as Your Database, Lesson 7: asked about our own retailer with nothing to read. AIS Week 3 AIS, slides 4 and 6: field names are facts you look up. READING Bonus Technical Lecture Notes, slides 49 and 89.

questions.stem: What belongs in Stage B of instruction tuning? In Figure 2, which activity belongs in Stage B of the instruction-tuning process taught in the lecture? (Figure 2. Instruction tuning, applied on top of a pre-trained model: Base model (pre-trained to predict the next token) -> Stage A (people write the answers; fine-tuning) -> Stage B (blank) -> Stage C (the model is nudged to higher scores; no person answers) -> Assistant (follows instructions).)
options: Retrieve a web page for every future user question.
Ask humans to rewrite every response produced after deployment.
Choose the most common answer from multiple inference-time samples.
Train a reward model using human rankings of candidate answers.
why: ✗ fetching a web page for each question is retrieval at answer time; it is not a training stage.
✗ no stage has people rewrite answers after deployment. People write answers only in Stage A, before release.
✗ choosing the most common of several samples is self-consistency, which runs after training as test-time compute.
✓ in Stage B the model writes several answers to each question, people only rank them, and a second model learns to predict the ranking: the reward model, a stand-in judge.
questions.explanation: Stage B is where a reward model is trained on people's rankings of candidate answers. Stage A: people write answers (the model learns the habit of answering). Stage B: people rank the model's answers and a second model learns the ranking. Stage C: the reward model scores new answers with no person present. Stages B and C together are RLHF.
questions.trap: C ('Choose the most common answer from multiple inference-time samples'). Self-consistency (choosing the most common of several samples) is a real course term. But it runs after training as test-time compute; it is not a training stage.
questions.tip: Stage A = people write; Stage B = people rank, and a reward model learns the ranking; Stage C = the judge scores, no person answers.
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 3 Lecture, slides 8, 10 and 12: people rank, a machine learns to rank; the reward model. LECTURE Week 1 Part 2 (PDF), pp. 16-24 and 34: ranking answers; Steps 2 and 3 are called RLHF. PROBLEM SET Problem Set 4, section B: where the agreeableness of coding agents comes from. QUIZ Review Quiz, Weeks 1 to 3, items 10 to 12, on the three-step figure.

questions.stem: Which example shows reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards? Which example best illustrates reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), as discussed in MGMT 6110 Human-AI Collaboration?
options: Score generated code by running it against specified test cases.
Score a business strategy only by how inspiring it sounds.
Reward an answer solely because it includes reasoning tags.
Ask the model to declare that its own answer is correct.
why: ✓ the loop is the same as RLHF (questions in, several answers out, each scored, model nudged towards high scores); RLVR changes only the judge: a rule compares with the known result, or runs the code against its tests.
✗ how inspiring a strategy sounds is a matter of taste with no answer key, so nothing can be verified.
✗ rewarding the tags alone is reward hacking. DeepSeek's format reward sits beside a check of the answer itself.
✗ a model that declares itself correct has verified nothing. The check has to come from outside: a key or a test.
questions.explanation: Scoring code by running it against test cases is RLVR (reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards). The loop is the same as RLHF, but a rule (known result or test) replaces the reward model as judge. Code either passes its tests or not, which is why coding and maths improved fastest; where no check exists, RLVR has nothing to score.
questions.trap: C ('Reward an answer solely because it includes reasoning tags'). DeepSeek did reward a reasoning format, so this sounds familiar. But rewarding the tags alone is reward hacking: nothing checks the answer itself.
questions.tip: Verifiable reward = an outside check gives the score: a known result or code run against its tests. If nothing outside can check it, it is not RLVR.
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 3 Lecture, slides 25-27: how the reward is computed; RLHF against RLVR. LECTURE Week 1 Part 2 (PDF), pp. 84-100: reinforcement learning with chain of thought; this is called RLVR. QUIZ Review Quiz, Weeks 1 to 3, item 19: rewards answers that pass an automatic check. READING Week 3 Bonus, slides 8 and 9: where each method runs out.

questions.stem: What does pre-training teach the model to estimate? During next-token pre-training, what is a GPT-style language model primarily trained to estimate?
options: A probability distribution over the next token, given preceding tokens.
The user's preferred answer, using live feedback on every token.
The probability that an entire answer is factually correct.
The exact number of times each complete sentence appears online.
why: ✓ at each of billions of positions in real text the model predicts the next token from the tokens before it, and its parameters are adjusted so the true token gets more probability; it learns a full distribution over its vocabulary.
✗ human preference enters later, through rankings collected offline in Step 2, never as live feedback on every token.
✗ nothing in the objective checks truth, which is why a fluent answer can be wrong.
✗ the model does not count sentences. Its probabilities are learned, and it scores sequences it has never seen.
questions.explanation: Pre-training teaches a probability distribution over the next token, given the tokens before it. That is why it finishes 'Peanut butter and' with 'jelly', and why a base model continues text instead of answering. 'Knowledge arrives in pre-training; the later steps change behaviour.'
questions.trap: C ('The probability that an entire answer is factually correct'). Many people assume a model is trained to be right. Nothing in pre-training checks truth; it learns a probability distribution over the next token.
questions.tip: Pre-training = next-token distribution given the tokens before. Human preferences come later (rankings). Truth is never in the objective.
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 1 Part 1 (PDF), pp. 39-42 and 54-55: trained to predict the next token; learned probabilities. LECTURE Week 3 Lecture, slides 6-8: it is finishing your paragraph; knowledge arrived in pre-training. NOTEBOOK AI+Py Day, Weeks 4 to 5 (27 September), Probes 4 and 5: the row that is not there; the wall at the end of the training data. READING Bonus Technical Lecture Notes, slides 21, 27, 28 and 63, for revision.

questions.official: Quiz 2 · Q6 — The five-part master prompt
questions.stem: How do you repair the prompt 'build a nice dashboard'? Which revision best improves the vague prompt 'Build a nice dashboard', using the course's Role, Goal, Output, Guardrails, Context Framework?
options: Ask for as many features as possible so the AI can choose the product
List preferred colours but omit what the user needs to accomplish.
Add "You are the world's best developer" and leave the rest unchanged.
Name the user and job, specify observable outcomes and deliverables and state constraints and context
why: ✗ asking for every feature hands the product decision to the agent and leaves no Guardrails.
✗ colours are cosmetic. Without the user and the job there is no Goal and no test of done.
✗ a Role line buys nothing on its own while the other four parts stay blank.
✓ the best revision names the user and the job, the observable outcomes and deliverables, and the constraints and context, i.e. fills all five parts.
questions.explanation: The best repair fills all five parts of the master prompt: Goal says what exists when done, in the user's words; Output names the files and the check that says done; Guardrails say what it must not do; Context gives audience and setting; Role comes last. Any part you leave blank, the model fills with what was most common in its training text.
questions.trap: C ('Add "You are the world's best developer" and leave the rest unchanged'). A strong Role line is the most famous prompt trick. But Role alone buys nothing while Goal, Output, Guardrails and Context stay blank.
questions.tip: Pick the option that fills all five parts: Role, Goal, Output, Guardrails, Context. Write the Goal first, Role last.
questions.source: Where we met it: AIS Week 2 AIS, slides 10-12: the five parts, and the order to write them in. PROBLEM SET Problem Set 1, section 2: Build a nice dashboard for my app, the weak Goal. AIS Week 2 AIS, slide 36: A [user] opens this screen to [one job], and knows it worked when [what they see]. PROBLEM SET Problem Set 2, panel 4: the back-end master prompt, with a longer Guardrails block.

questions.official: Quiz 2 · Q2 — Where an API key lives
questions.stem: Where should the secret key be stored and used? A product uses a third-party API that requires a secret key. In Figure 3, where should that key be stored and used? (Figure 3. A product calls an API that needs a secret key: PUBLIC, the visitor's territory = Browser (the page, its URL and its downloaded JavaScript); THE KITCHEN, machines you control = Back end (a serverless function on Vercel, deployed from GitHub); THE PROVIDER, outside your product = Third-party API (answers only requests that carry the secret key).)
options: In the browser URL so every request can include it.
In the browser's downloadable JavaScript.
In a server-side environment variable, used by the product's back end.
In the public GitHub repository beside the source code.
why: ✗ a key in the URL shows in the address bar, in browser history and in server logs.
✗ every visitor can read the downloaded JavaScript, including any VITE_ variable that the build writes into it.

✓ anything in the front end is public; so the page calls your own address (e.g. /api/bus) and your serverless function on Vercel reads the key from an environment variable, adds it to the request and returns only the answer.
✗ public repositories are scanned within minutes, and Git history keeps the key after you delete it. Rotate it first, tidy second.
questions.explanation: The key belongs in a server-side environment variable used only by the back end. The front end is public (the browser downloads it and View Source shows all of it), so the page calls your own /api route and the serverless function adds the key. In the Week 3 studio this was LTA_ACCOUNT_KEY, saved in Vercel as Secret, followed by a redeploy.
questions.trap: B ('In the browser's downloadable JavaScript'). Putting the key in the app's own code feels private. But every visitor downloads that JavaScript, including any VITE_ variable written in at build time.
questions.tip: Ask: 'Does the browser need to know it?' For a credential the answer is never. Key = server-side environment variable read only by your back-end function.
questions.source: Where we met it: AIS Week 3 AIS, slides 7 and 13: which way the request travels, and where a key leaks. AIS Week 2 AIS, slides 8 and 9: front end and back end; a key in the front end is published. PROBLEM SET Problem Set 2, panels 3 to 5: every key inside api/ only; LTA_ACCOUNT_KEY saved in Vercel as Secret. Week 3 Singapore API Card, Overview: keys live in Vercel, calls live in /api.

questions.stem: The API requires a secret key. In the architecture shown, where should the product store and use that key? (Figure: Browser (front end) -> Back end: a server-side function on Vercel -> Third-party API (needs a secret key); a Public GitHub repository deploys to the back end; 'Where does the key go?')
options: In a server-side environment variable used only by the product's back end, for example a server-side function hosted on Vercel.
In a query string displayed in the browser address bar.
Inside the browser's downloadable JavaScript.
In the public repository so deployment can find it.
why: ✓ 'The key belongs in a server-side environment variable that only the product's back end reads, such as a function on Vercel.'
✗ 'A query string shows in the address bar and is kept in logs and history; our API card puts keys in a header, never in the URL.'
✗ 'Anything in the downloadable JavaScript can be read with View Source, including any VITE_ variable written in at build time.'
✗ 'Public repositories are scanned within minutes, and git history keeps a key after the file is deleted; Vercel holds the key.'
questions.explanation: Anyone who holds the key can spend your quota and act in your name, and the browser, the page address and a public repository can all be read by strangers. In the Week 3 studio the LTA AccountKey sat in a Vercel environment variable set as a Secret, read only inside the function in the api folder, while the page called our own /api/bus. Quiz 2, Question 2 asked the same.
questions.trap: D ('In the public repository so deployment can find it'). 'So deployment can find it' sounds practical. But public repositories are scanned within minutes, and git history keeps a key after you delete it.
questions.tip: Same answer every time: a server-side environment variable read only by the back end (a Vercel Secret). If a key leaks: rotate first, tidy second.
questions.source: Where we met it: AIS Week 3 AIS, slides 7, 12 and 13 (which way the request travels; what a key is; where a key leaks); AIS Week 3 AIS, slides 14 and 15 (the rules that keep it private; the three stations); PROBLEM SET Problem Set 2, sections 3 and 5 (credentials inside api/ only; Vercel holds the key); GUIDE Week 3 Singapore API Card (keys go in a header, on the server side only).

questions.stem: Does using the help widget predict success? A manager claims that using a help widget predicts successful task completion. What does Figure 4 show? (Figure 4. Task completion by help-widget use (users): Used the help widget: succeeded 80, failed 20, total 100. Did not use the widget: succeeded 40, failed 10, total 50. Total: 120, 30, 150.)
options: The claim is supported because 80 users both used the widget and succeeded.
The widget reduced success because 20 widget users failed.
Success is 80% in both groups, so this table shows no association between widget use and success.
The claim is supported because the diagonal cells contain 60% of users.
why: ✗ this counts the one cell that agrees with the claim. The 80 has to be set against the non-users' 40 in 50.
✗ twenty failures in 100 users is a 20% failure rate, the same as 10 in 50 for non-users.
✓ compare the rows: widget users succeed 80 in 100 = 80%, non-users 40 in 50 = 80%. The cross-products agree: 80 x 10 and 20 x 40 both come to 800.
✗ the diagonal, 90 of 150, is the confirmation method. With both events this common, 60% is what unrelated events would give.
questions.explanation: Success is 80% in both rows, so the table shows no association between widget use and success. To test a claim, ask what would prove it wrong (non-users succeeding as often as users) and compare the success RATE in each row. This is the Week 4 symptom table with new labels; reading only the 80 is the confirmation method (confirmation bias).
questions.trap: A ('The claim is supported because 80 users both used the widget and succeeded'). 80 widget users who succeeded is the biggest number in the table, so it looks like proof. It is one cell: the confirmation method.
questions.tip: Two-by-two table: compute the rate in each row and compare. Equal rates (80% and 80%) = no association. Never read one cell or the diagonal.
questions.source: Where we met it: PROBLEM SET Problem Set 4, section C: the table from our Week 4 lesson, 80 and 20 against 40 and 10. LECTURE Week 4 lesson, The Human Side of the Collaboration: Confirmation Bias (its table is reproduced in Problem Set 4). PROBLEM SET Problem Set 4, section E and Step 4: the falsification method and the four-way table. QUIZ Quiz 3, Question 8, and Quiz 4, Question 10, return to the same idea.

questions.official: Quiz 2 · Q8 — Recognition rather than recall
questions.stem: Which heuristic removes the memory burden? A bus app requires visitors to remember and type an exact stop name. It offers no visible list, suggestions, or recent choices. Which heuristic most directly addresses that memory burden?
options: Visibility of System Status
Recognition Rather than Recall
User Control and Freedom
Aesthetic and Minimalist Design
why: ✗ Visibility of System Status is about what is happening now, such as loading or the age of the data.
✓ heuristic 6 asks whether people can see the options or must remember them; Nielsen's wording is to minimise the user's memory load by making elements, actions and options visible.
✗ User Control and Freedom is about a way back from a mistake: back, undo and cancel.
✗ Aesthetic and Minimalist Design removes what competes for attention; removing suggestions would make recall harder.
questions.explanation: Recognition Rather than Recall (Nielsen heuristic 6: 'Can they see the options, or must they remember them?') removes the memory burden. Typing an exact stop name with no list, suggestions or recent choices puts the memory on the person. The repair is a suggestion list, recent stops and visible filters, with the server sending each stop's name beside its code.
questions.trap: A ('Visibility of System Status'). Visibility of System Status is the most familiar heuristic. But it is about what is happening now (loading, data age), not memory load.
questions.tip: Memory burden (type it exactly, no list) = Recognition Rather than Recall (heuristic 6): 'Can they see the options, or must they remember them?'
questions.source: Where we met it: AIS Week 5 AIS, slides 4, 23 and 24: heuristic 6, show the options instead of expecting them to be recalled. PROBLEM SET Problem Set 4, section D, row 6: a visitor has to type a stop exactly as the provider spells it. AIS Week 5 AIS, slides 10, 16 and 27: the heuristics behind the wrong options. AIS Week 3 AIS: the LTA bus-arrival build the case comes from.

questions.official: Quiz 2 · Q10 — Visibility of system status
questions.stem: A cached forecast labelled Live: what is the repair? In Figure 6, the provider failed at 12:00 and the back end returned a cached 08:00 forecast. The screen labels it 'Live'. Which repair best addresses the problem? (Figure 6. The forecast a visitor sees at 12:05: 08:00 the back end fetches the forecast and caches it; 12:00 the provider call fails and the back end returns the cached 08:00 forecast. Card: 'Weather for the 1 PM site visit [Live] 31°C, thunderstorms after 2 PM'. No time, source or failure notice is shown.)
options: Hide all status information to keep the screen minimal.
Change the displayed timestamp to 12:00 because that was the request time.
Return source, observation time, and cache status from the back end; show the age and failure state clearly on screen.
Use a brighter colour for "Live".
why: ✗ hiding the status removes the facts the person acts on. Minimalism removes what is irrelevant.
✗ 12:00 was the time of the request, so relabelling it makes the false claim more precise.

✓ heuristic 1 asks a design to keep people informed about what is going on; the response carries when the reading was taken and which source answered, a cached answer says so and how old it is, and a failure is reported.
✗ a brighter Live label makes the false claim louder. The label itself is the defect.
questions.explanation: The repair is split between server and screen: the back end returns source, observation time and cache status, and the screen shows the data's age and the failure. This is Visibility of System Status (heuristic 1): a forecast read at 08:00 and shown at 12:00 as Live misinforms exactly when it matters. If the back end never sends these facts, no care on the screen can show them.
questions.trap: B ('Change the displayed timestamp to 12:00 because that was the request time'). Changing the timestamp feels like being more precise. But 12:00 was the request time, so it makes the false 'Live' claim more precise, not true.
questions.tip: Visibility of System Status (heuristic 1): the back end must send source, observation time and cache status; the screen shows the age and the failure.
questions.source: Where we met it: AIS Week 5 AIS, slides 10, 12 and 31: freshness is data; a forecast with no clock; the stale cache. AIS Week 3 AIS, slides 20 and 22: the health endpoint with lastGoodFetch; why you cache. PROBLEM SET Problem Set 2, panel 4: four sentences for loading, empty, refused and unreachable. PROBLEM SET Problem Set 4, section D: a reading appears with no sign of when it was taken.

questions.stem: Inspect the two findings in the figure. Which pairing best matches each finding to its primary Nielsen heuristic? Finding A (the departure board): the crowding column shows SEA, SDA and LSD, the codes sent by the bus feed; visitors ask what the letters mean. Finding B (arrival times): the same bus is shown as 4.37 min in the list, 9:52 am on its card and 2026-10-21T09:52 in the alert.
options: A: User Control and Freedom; B: Help and Documentation.
A: Match Between the System and the Real World; B: Consistency and Standards.
A: Flexibility and Efficiency of Use; B: Error Prevention.
A: Consistency and Standards; B: Match Between the System and the Real World.
why: ✗ 'Neither finding is about a way back from a mistake, which is User Control and Freedom, or about help at the moment it is needed.'

✓ Match asks whether the words on screen are the users' words or the database's (codes copied from the feed); Consistency asks whether the same thing always looks and behaves the same way (one arrival time written three ways).
✗ 'Neither finding is about a faster path for regular users or about a design that makes a mistake impossible.'
✗ 'This swaps the two: words from the database break Match, and one thing written in different ways breaks Consistency.'
questions.explanation: Heuristic 2, Match Between the System and the Real World, asks 'Are the words theirs, or the database's?' - SEA/SDA/LSD are raw feed codes where people expect plain words (e.g. 'Seats available'). Heuristic 4, Consistency and Standards, asks 'Does the same thing always look and behave the same way?' - one arrival time is written three different ways. Prof. Roh's tip: 'Ask first whether a user would say the word, then whether the product always says it the same way.'
questions.trap: D ('A: Consistency and Standards; B: Match Between the System and the Real World'). Both heuristics are about words on screen, so swapping them is easy. Raw database codes break Match; one time written three ways breaks Consistency.
questions.tip: First ask 'Would a user say this word?' (Match, heuristic 2). Then 'Does the product always say it the same way?' (Consistency and Standards, heuristic 4).
questions.source: Where we met it: AIS Week 5 AIS, slide 4 (the ten heuristics and the question each one asks); Week 5 AIS, slides 14 to 19 (Match: SEA, SDA and LSD; Consistency: three ways of writing a time); PROBLEM SET Problem Set 4, Section D (the ten heuristics, rows 2 and 4); Week 5 AIS, slide 38 (the clinic, six-line findings on a classmate's Disqus board).

questions.official: Quiz 3 · Q5 — User control and freedom
questions.stem: An AI rewrite follows the flow shown. Which redesign best supports User Control and Freedom? (Flow: Original paragraph -> The person presses Rewrite with AI -> The AI version replaces the original -> No undo, compare or restore.)
options: Preserve the original, offer comparison, and allow restoration.
Show a confirmation after the original has already been lost.
Use a more capable model but preserve the same irreversible process.
Hide the rewrite button after the first use.
why: ✓ 'Keeping the original, offering a comparison and allowing restoration is the redesign that supports User Control and Freedom.'
✗ 'A confirmation after the original is gone gives no way back; an action that cannot be reversed is confirmed before it happens.'
✗ 'A more capable model still writes rewrites that people regret, and the flow still destroys the original.'
✗ 'Hiding the button takes control away from the person and leaves the first rewrite irreversible.'
questions.explanation: Heuristic 3, User Control and Freedom, asks 'Is there a way back from a mistake?' In the flow shown, the AI version replaces the original, so the earlier text is lost (the Problem Set 4 table uses this case for heuristic 3). The repair keeps the original, lets the person compare both versions and restores the original in one step - like the Undo in the Week 5 studio that brought back a saved bus stop removed by mistake.
questions.trap: B ('Show a confirmation after the original has already been lost'). A confirmation dialog sounds like control. But a confirmation after the original is gone gives no way back; an action that cannot be reversed is confirmed before it happens.
questions.tip: User Control and Freedom (heuristic 3) = 'Is there a way back from a mistake?' Keep the original, let people compare, restore in one step.
questions.source: Where we met it: PROBLEM SET Problem Set 4, Section D, row 3 (once the model rewrites something, the earlier version is lost); AIS Week 5 AIS, slides 16 and 17 (User Control and Freedom; give every action a way back); AIS Week 5 AIS, slide 5 (this deck judged by the ten, with Esc and Backspace as ways back); AIS Week 7 routines deck, slide 5 (can we take it back?).

questions.stem: A manager says the help widget predicts task success because 80 widget users succeeded. What does the full table support? (Table: Used the help widget - Succeeded 80, Did not succeed 20, Total 100; Did not use it - 40, 10, 50; Total - 120, 30, 150.)
options: Success is 80% in both groups; the table shows no association.
Non-users are less successful because their total is smaller.
The two diagonal counts prove the widget works.
The widget caused higher success because 80 is larger than 40.
why: ✓ 'Success is 80% in both groups, so the table shows no association.' (80/100 = 80%; 40/50 = 80%.)
✗ 'A smaller group is not a less successful one; 40 of 50 is the same rate as 80 of 100.'
✗ 'The diagonal, 80 and 10, is what the confirmation method counts; its 60% is the agreement expected when the two are unrelated.'
✗ '80 and 40 come from groups of different sizes, and a table like this could not show cause even if the rates differed.'
questions.explanation: To test a claim like this, compare the success rate in each row: widget users 80/100 = 80%, non-users 40/50 = 80%, so there is no association. The manager counted only the cell that agrees with the belief (the confirmation method from the Week 4 lesson); the falsification method compares the rows. The diagonal (80 + 10 = 90 of 150 = 60%) is just the agreement you would expect by chance. Quiz 2, Question 3 used the same table.
questions.trap: C ('The two diagonal counts prove the widget works'). The diagonal (80 + 10) looks like 'agreement with the claim'. Its 60% is the agreement you would expect when the two things are unrelated.
questions.tip: Rates per row: 80/100 = 80% and 40/50 = 80%. Same rate = no association. Even different rates would show association, not cause.
questions.source: Where we met it: PROBLEM SET Problem Set 4, Section C (the table from our Week 4 lesson, with both methods worked out); LECTURE Week 4 lesson, 16 September (confirmation bias, worked through with a two-by-two table); LECTURE Week 7 Lecture, slide 3 (agreement is the weakest evidence); QUIZ Quiz 2, Question 3 (the same table).

questions.stem: An employee expense form accepts a negative headcount and submits it without warning. The global service team wants to stop this mistake before it reaches an approver. Which change most directly applies Error Prevention?
options: Move the help manual to the first page.
Reject invalid headcounts and explain the allowed values before submission.
Add an undo button to the approval email.
Use the same colour for all fields.
why: ✗ 'A manual on the first page is Help and Documentation, and it still lets a negative number through.'
✓ Rejecting invalid headcounts and explaining the allowed values before submission applies Error Prevention.
✗ 'An undo in the approval email is User Control and Freedom: a way back after the mistake has already reached the approver.'
✗ 'One colour for every field checks nothing, and it makes the fields harder to tell apart.'
questions.explanation: Error Prevention (heuristic 5) asks whether the mistake could have been made impossible: remove the error-prone condition, or check for it before the person commits. Rejecting a negative headcount as it is entered, and stating the allowed values, stops the slip on the screen, and the same check on the server stops it there. The mistake never reaches the approver, which is what the team asked for.
questions.trap: C ('Add an undo button to the approval email'). An undo button is a good feature. But undo in the approval email is User Control and Freedom: a way back AFTER the mistake has reached the approver.
questions.tip: Error Prevention (heuristic 5) = 'Could the mistake have been made impossible?' Check the entry before the person commits, on screen and again on the server.
questions.source: Where we met it: AIS Week 5 AIS, slide 20 (Error Prevention, on the screen and on the server); AIS Week 5 AIS, slides 4 and 21 (the ten heuristics and the question each asks; make the wrong entry impossible); PROBLEM SET Problem Set 4 (your heuristic evaluation, with the heuristic named in each finding); Week 8 AIS kit, uni-site-audit: HEURISTICS.md, heuristic 5.

questions.stem: A consulting team asks a model to assess a market-entry proposal. Its first prompt says, 'Explain why our expansion will succeed.' Which follow-up would best address confirmation bias?
options: Ask what evidence would overturn the proposal, then check that evidence.
Rewrite the favourable answer in a more cautious tone.
Ask three times and keep the answer that agrees most strongly.
Add the managing partner's support to the prompt.
why: ✓ 'The team should ask what evidence would overturn the proposal, and then check that evidence.'
✗ 'A more cautious tone changes the wording, while the answer still rests only on the cases that agree.'
✗ 'Keeping the answer that agrees most is confirmation bias itself. As Week 7 said, agreement is the weakest evidence.'
✗ 'The partner's support tells the model which answer is wanted. It adds authority and no evidence.'
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias is 'our habit of looking for the cases that agree with what we believe and seldom for the ones that could prove it wrong.' The first prompt asks only for support, and an assistant trained on human preferences tends to move towards a user's stated view (sycophancy). Asking what would overturn the proposal, then checking it against its source (e.g. competitor price list, draft agreements, pilot sales data), is the falsification method of Week 4 and of predictions.md in Problem Set 4.
questions.trap: C ('Ask three times and keep the answer that agrees most strongly'). Asking several times sounds thorough. But keeping the answer that agrees most is confirmation bias itself: agreement is the weakest evidence.
questions.tip: Fix confirmation bias by asking what would prove the belief wrong, then checking that evidence against its source (the falsification method).
questions.source: Where we met it: PROBLEM SET Problem Set 4, section C (confirmation bias in the table from class; ask what would prove the belief wrong); PROBLEM SET Problem Set 4, Step 2 (predictions.md, with the one finding that would show your evaluation was wrong); LECTURE Week 7 Lecture, slide 26 (agreement is the weakest evidence); LECTURE Co-Collaboration Model deck, slides 12 and 17 (an agreeable assistant can plant a false consensus).

questions.stem: A retail chain's marketing lead says customers who use its loyalty app come back more, because 90 app users made a repeat purchase last quarter. The full table: app users, 90 repeat and 30 no repeat; non-users, 40 repeat and 40 no repeat. Define confirmation bias, read the table, and say what the chain should check before it spends more on the app.

table.note: Totals and rates computed in the model answer.

parts.label: (a)
parts.task: Define confirmation bias.
parts.model: Confirmation bias is our habit of looking for the cases that agree with what we already believe, and seldom for the ones that could prove us wrong.

parts.label: (b)
parts.task: Explain the confirmation vs falsification method.
parts.model: Counting the agreeing cell, 90 app users who came back, is the confirmation method. The falsification method uses all four cells and compares the rate in each row.

parts.label: (c)
parts.task: Read (apply to) the table.
parts.model: App users: 90 of 120 = 75%. Non-users: 40 of 80 = 50%. The rates differ, so the table shows an association between app use and repeat purchase. The diagonal, 90 + 40 = 130 of 200, is not the test.

parts.label: (d)
parts.task: Say what the chain should check before spending more.
parts.model: An association does not show that the app causes the repeat purchase, because loyal customers may be the ones who install it. The chain should test it, for example by offering the app to a random half of new customers and comparing their repeat rates.

questions.modelAnswer: (a) Confirmation bias is our habit of looking for the cases that agree with what we already believe, and seldom for the ones that could prove us wrong. (b) Counting the agreeing cell, 90 app users who came back, is the confirmation method. The falsification method uses all four cells and compares the rate in each row. (c) App users: 90 of 120 = 75%. Non-users: 40 of 80 = 50%. The rates differ, so the table shows an association between app use and repeat purchase. The diagonal, 90 + 40 = 130 of 200, is not the test. (d) An association does not show that the app causes the repeat purchase, because loyal customers may be the ones who install it. The chain should test it, for example by offering the app to a random half of new customers and comparing their repeat rates.
questions.explanation: Define: looking for the cases that agree with a belief, and seldom for those that could disprove it. Explain: the count of 90 is the confirmation method; the falsification method compares the rate in each row. Apply: compute 90 of 120 = 75% against 40 of 80 = 50%, and say the table shows an association. Check: an association is not a cause; name a test, such as offering the app to a random half of new customers.
questions.trap: Reporting 90 as the evidence, or adding the diagonal. Compute the rate in each row.
questions.tip: Show your working where there is a number (p.152).
questions.source: Where we met it: Problem Set 4, Section C: the table from our Week 4 lesson; Quiz 2, Question 3, and Quiz 3, Question 8; Lecture: Week 4: confirmation bias and the falsification method

questions.official: Quiz 3 · Q6 — Generative and agentic AI
questions.stem: A marketing manager uses AI in two ways in the same week: Scenario X: They ask an AI chatbot to draft a product-launch email, edit the draft, paste it into Outlook and send it themselves. Scenario Y: They tell an AI assistant, 'Set up a 30-minute meeting with the three regional leads next week.' It checks calendars, sends invites, and finds a new time when one lead declines. Which statement is correct?
options: Y is agentic AI, because the AI acts in other systems, reacts to the decline and keeps going until done.
Both are generative AI, because both are powered by the same kind of large language model.
Y is generative AI, because a calendar invite is another piece of content the AI produced.
X is agentic AI, because the AI wrote the entire email without any help from the manager.
why: ✓ 'Y is agentic AI, because the AI acts in other systems, reacts to the decline and keeps going until the job is done.'
✗ 'The same model can sit inside a chatbot or inside an agent; the software around it decides whether it can act.'
✗ 'Sending invites changes calendars in other people's systems, which is acting in the world rather than producing content.'
✗ 'Writing a whole email is still generating text; the manager edited and sent it, so the AI acted in no system.'
questions.explanation: In X the AI writes and the manager does everything that follows (edits, pastes, sends), so it is generative AI. In Y the AI checks calendars, sends invites, reads the decline and goes round again until a time works - 'a model in a loop that reads, chooses and acts through tools'. Both can run on the same kind of model; the loop and the tools around it make Y agentic.
questions.trap: B ('Both are generative AI, because both are powered by the same kind of large language model'). Both scenarios do run on the same kind of model, so it sounds true. But the software around the model decides whether it can act.
questions.tip: Agentic = acts in other systems + reacts to what comes back + keeps going until done. Writing a whole email is still generating text.
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 5 Lecture (revised), slides 24, 28 and 30 (generation and agency can coexist; the agent loop; how text becomes an action); LECTURE Week 7 Lecture, slides 7, 8 and 10 (sense, decide, act; Is it an agent?; one request round the loop); AIS Week 7 Zapier AIS, slide 12 (fixed steps or a chosen step); READING Week 8 Lecture, slide 11, for revision (fetching changes nothing, while acting changes a record).

questions.stem: The agent starts only when a new form is submitted. Its job and report are shown. Which component is the trigger? (Figure: 1 A new form is submitted -> 2 Job: classify the form into a category -> 3 Report saved: the form and its category label.)
options: The new-form-submitted event.
The instruction to classify the form.
The report saved after processing.
The category labels in the output.
why: ✓ A trigger is the event that starts a run, and this agent starts only when a new form is submitted.
✗ 'The instruction tells the agent what to do once it is running; it does not start the run.'
✗ 'The report is the output at the end of a run, so it comes after the trigger.'
✗ 'The category labels are part of the output that the job produces.'
questions.explanation: A trigger is the event that starts a run - here, a new form being submitted. Classifying the form is the job the agent does once running, and the report with category labels is the output at the end. The Problem Set 5 agent card keeps these on separate lines: the job, the trigger, the tools, what it must never do, and where a person checks.
questions.trap: B ('The instruction to classify the form'). The instruction is the first thing the agent 'does', so it feels like the start. But a trigger is the event that starts a run; the instruction is the job once running.
questions.tip: Trigger = the EVENT that starts a run (a person, a schedule or an event). Job = what it does. Report/labels = the output.
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 6 Lecture, slide 15 (what starts a run when nobody is there? A person, a schedule or an event); AIS Week 7 Zapier AIS, slides 5 and 13 (the parts of a Zap; what makes an agent autonomous); AIS Week 7, Your First AI Agent with Claude Routines, slides 6 and 8 (a routine is a saved prompt plus a trigger); PROBLEM SET Problem Set 5: the agent card, line 2, the trigger.

questions.official: Quiz 3 · Q1 — The map: a person decides
questions.stem: A consultant chooses a negotiation strategy for a client. Several strategies are reasonable, and the consultant can complete the task independently. AI may suggest alternatives, but no joint human-AI process is required. Which placement and arrangement fit the course map? (Figure: blank 2x2 map, columns 'Work with a right answer' / 'Work with no single right answer', rows 'Work that people and AI must do together' / 'Work that either of them can do alone'; place: a consultant chooses a negotiation strategy for a client.)
options: Right answer + must work together: a person signs off a mechanically checkable answer.
No single right answer + must work together: using any AI suggestion makes joint work mandatory.
No single right answer + either can work alone: a person decides, with AI alongside.
Right answer + either can work alone: AI selects the uniquely correct strategy.
why: ✗ 'A right answer would mean one strategy could be checked mechanically, and the stem says several strategies are reasonable.'
✗ 'Taking an AI suggestion does not make the task joint work; the top row is for work that people and AI must do together.'
✓ 'The task has no single right answer and either of them can do it alone, so a person decides, with AI alongside.'
✗ 'There is no uniquely correct strategy for AI to select, and the consultant answers for the advice.'
questions.explanation: The Week 7 Map of Human-AI Collaboration asks two questions of every task: (1) does it have a right answer? (2) must people and AI do it together, or can either do it alone? Several strategies are reasonable, so there is no single right answer (right-hand column); the consultant can finish alone (bottom row). That is the bottom-right quadrant, 'A person decides, AI alongside'. In class the same task was a banker planning a hard client negotiation while AI drafts options and the banker decides.
questions.trap: B ('No single right answer + must work together: using any AI suggestion makes joint work mandatory'). AI suggests options, so it feels like joint work. But taking an AI suggestion does not make the work joint; the top row is only for work people and AI MUST do together.
questions.tip: Ask the map's two questions in order. 'Several strategies are reasonable' = no single right answer. 'Can complete independently' = either can do it alone. That is 'A person decides, AI alongside'.
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 7, The Map of Human-AI Collaboration, slide 3 (a person decides with AI alongside; a banker plans a client negotiation); LECTURE Week 7 Map deck, slides 4 and 5 (examples across functions; Place the task, Bank, Plan a negotiation); AIS Week 7 studio team build, Agents x Quadrant; PROBLEM SET Problem Set 5, Step 3 (what each quadrant means for the person in the loop) and Q1 (a) to (d).

questions.official: Quiz 3 · Q3 — The map: AI alone, with checks
questions.stem: A finance team checks whether each payment matches an invoice using the exact rules in the figure. AI can complete routine cases without human participation; staff only spot-check results and handle exceptions. Which placement and work arrangement fit the course map? (Matching rules: 1. The payment's invoice number matches an open invoice. 2. The amount matches to the cent. 3. Paid within 30 days. All three met: matched. Any rule failed: exception queue, handled by staff.)
options: No single right answer + either can work alone: a person decides with AI alongside.
Right answer + must work together: a person must lead every routine match.
Right answer + either can work alone: AI performs the routine task, with spot checks.
No single right answer + must work together: agents run the task and a person judges every match.
why: ✗ 'A person deciding with AI alongside is for work with no single right answer, and here the rules decide each match.'
✗ 'The top-left quadrant keeps a person leading where the firm answers for each decision, such as a loan file; routine matches do not need that.'
✓ 'Each payment has one right match and AI can do the routine cases alone, so AI performs the task, with spot checks.'
✗ 'The task has a right answer, and a person judging every match would remove the reason to let AI do the routine cases.'
questions.explanation: Exact matching rules give each payment one right answer, and a wrong match is easy to catch, so the task sits in the left column ('Work with a right answer'). AI finishes routine cases without a person, so it is the bottom row ('Work that either of them can do alone'). The bottom-left quadrant is 'AI alone, with checks': AI matches, staff spot-check and handle the exception queue. It is the class example in the Bank row of the map.
questions.trap: B ('Right answer + must work together: a person must lead every routine match'). Finance work feels important enough for a person to lead. But exact rules give one right match and AI can do routine cases alone; a person on every match removes the reason to use AI.
questions.tip: Exact rules + routine cases done alone + staff spot-check and handle exceptions = 'AI alone, with checks' (bottom-left).
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 7 Map deck, slide 3, step 3 (AI does it, with spot checks; a finance team's AI matches payments to invoices); slide 5 (Payments, Match payments to invoices); slide 3, step 6 (our news-watch agent sits bottom left); PROBLEM SET Problem Set 5, Step 3 (bottom left, AI matches incoming payments to invoices).

questions.official: Quiz 3 · Q9 — The map: agents run it, a person judges
questions.stem: Agents cluster user comments and prepare alternative product priorities. The PM must choose among competing goals, with no single right ranking. Which map placement fits? (Flow: User comments from the app store -> Agents cluster them into themes -> Agents prepare priority options -> The PM weighs the goals and chooses.)
options: No single answer; agents run the process and a person judges inside it.
Right answer; AI alone.
Right answer; no judgement needed.
No single answer; the human must do every processing step alone.
why: ✓ 'The task has no single answer and needs both, so agents run the process and a person judges inside it.'
✗ 'There is no right ranking to check against, so AI alone with spot checks does not fit.'
✗ 'The task turns on judgement between competing goals, so a placement that needs no judgement misreads it.'
✗ 'The agents already do the processing here, and the map keeps the person at the judgement points rather than at every step.'
questions.explanation: Ranking product priorities has no single right answer because the PM must weigh competing goals (right column). Agents do the processing (clustering comments, preparing options) but the choice stays with the PM, so people and AI must work on it together (top row).
