That is the top-right quadrant, 'Agents run it, a person judges', with the PM judging inside the process at the decision point - the same class example: agents cluster user comments while the PM sets priorities.
questions.trap: D ('No single answer; the human must do every processing step alone'). Keeping the person on every step sounds safe. But agents already do the processing; the map keeps the person at the judgement points.
questions.tip: No single right answer + agents process + person chooses inside the process = 'Agents run it, a person judges' (top-right).
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 7 Map deck, slide 3, step 4 (agents cluster user comments while the PM sets priorities); LECTURE Week 7 Map deck, slides 5 and 6 (Product, Sort user comments; agents and the map); LECTURE Week 7 Lecture, slide 12 (the UK government's Consult sorts consultation responses into themes); PROBLEM SET Problem Set 5, Step 3 (top right, a person judges inside the process).

questions.official: Part B Practice 3 — The Week 7 map
questions.stem: An insurer wants AI on two tasks: (a) checking each expense claim against the written travel rules and flagging the ones that break a rule, and (b) choosing a brand ambassador for next year's campaign. Define the two questions of the Map of Human-AI Collaboration, place each task, and say what the person does in each.

parts.label: (a)
parts.task: Define the two questions of the Map of Human-AI Collaboration.
parts.model: The map asks two questions of each task: does it have a right answer, and is it work that people and AI must do together, or work that either of them can do alone? The two answers place the task in one of four quadrants.

parts.label: (b)
parts.task: Explain what the placement tells us.
parts.model: Where a task sits tells us who should lead it. We place tasks one at a time, never a whole job, and once agents help we also ask who answers for the result.

parts.label: (c)
parts.task: Place each task.
parts.model: (a) Each claim meets the written rules or does not, and AI can check routine claims alone, so it sits in AI alone, with checks. (b) No single ambassador is right, and a manager can choose alone with AI drafting the options, so it sits in A person decides, AI alongside.

parts.label: (d)
parts.task: Say what the person does in each.
parts.model: In (a) a person spot-checks a sample, handles every flagged claim, and sends the task back for review when the rules change. In (b) the manager decides and answers for the choice, and uses AI to list options and check facts about each candidate.

questions.modelAnswer: (a) The map asks two questions of each task: does it have a right answer, and is it work that people and AI must do together, or work that either of them can do alone? The two answers place the task in one of four quadrants. (b) Where a task sits tells us who should lead it. We place tasks one at a time, never a whole job, and once agents help we also ask who answers for the result. (c) (a) Each claim meets the written rules or does not, and AI can check routine claims alone, so it sits in AI alone, with checks. (b) No single ambassador is right, and a manager can choose alone with AI drafting the options, so it sits in A person decides, AI alongside. (d) In (a) a person spot-checks a sample, handles every flagged claim, and sends the task back for review when the rules change. In (b) the manager decides and answers for the choice, and uses AI to list options and check facts about each candidate.
questions.explanation: Define: the map's two questions, whether the task has a right answer and whether people and AI must do it together. Explain: the quadrant says who leads, one task at a time. Apply: place claim checking in AI alone, with checks and the ambassador in A person decides, AI alongside, with a reason for each. Check: what the person does in each task, such as spot checks and every flagged claim in (a), and the decision and the fact checks in (b).

questions.tip: Show your working where there is a placement (p.152).

questions.official: Quiz 3 · Q10 — Trigger and action in a Zap
questions.stem: A team wants Zapier to notify a Slack channel whenever a new response arrives in its survey form. In the workflow shown, which event is the trigger and which is the action? (Flow: Survey form: a new response arrives -> Zapier -> Slack: post the response summary to the channel.)
options: The survey response is an action; opening the Zap editor is the trigger.
Both events are triggers because both involve an app.
Trigger: a new survey response arrives; Action: post its summary to Slack.
Trigger: post the Slack message; Action: receive the survey response.
why: ✗ 'Opening the editor is how you build the Zap, not an event in an app; the survey response starts each run.'
✗ 'Both events involve an app, but only one starts the run; the Slack post is the step Zapier performs.'
✓ A Zap is one trigger and the steps after it: the new survey response starts the run; posting to Slack is what Zapier then does.
✗ 'This reverses the order, since the post can only happen after a response has arrived.'
questions.explanation: A Zap reads as WHEN the trigger happens, DO the actions. The trigger is the event that starts a run (a new response arriving in the survey form); the action is what Zapier then does in another app (posting a summary to Slack). In the Week 7 Zap the trigger was RSS by Zapier, New Item in Feed, and the action was Email by Zapier, Send Outbound Email; on the free plan only the action uses a task.
questions.trap: D ('Trigger: post the Slack message; Action: receive the survey response'). It reverses the order. The Slack post can only happen after a survey response arrives, so the response is the trigger.
questions.tip: Read a Zap as 'WHEN [trigger] happens, DO [action]'. Building the Zap is not a trigger.
questions.source: Where we met it: AIS Week 7 Zapier AIS, slides 2 and 5 (when this happens, do this; the parts of a Zap); Week 7 Zapier Exercises, slide 5 (Exercise 1, RSS by Zapier to Email by Zapier); GUIDE Week 7 Zapier Self-Study Guide (build a Zap when you can list every step before it runs); PROBLEM SET Problem Set 5 (your own Zap, three runs and its Zap history JSON).

questions.stem: A multinational distributor compares the two systems in Figure 1. Both start each morning without a person pressing Run. Which statement best explains the difference? (System A: a fixed scheduled sequence - every morning -> predict delay risk -> filter -> email; the same path every run. System B: a model chooses, reads and decides again - every morning -> the model -> choose a lookup -> read the result -> decide again ... -> stop rule.)
options: Both are agentic because a schedule starts them automatically.
System A uses a prediction inside a fixed workflow; System B shows an agentic loop because its model chooses tools and responds to their results.
System B is agentic only because it uses Claude rather than Zapier.
System A is agentic because sending an email is an action, while System B is predictive because it reads data.
why: ✗ 'A schedule is a trigger. It decides when a run starts, and says nothing about who chooses the steps inside the run.'
✓ 'System A puts a prediction inside a fixed workflow, while System B runs an agentic loop.'
✗ 'The vendor is not the test. A Zapier agent can choose its next step too, and Claude in a chat sits in Ask.'
✗ 'An email at the end of fixed steps is an automation's action. System B is not predictive either: it chooses lookups and decides again.'
questions.explanation: The test is who chooses the next step. In System A a person drew the steps (predict delay risk, filter, email) and the model only fills the prediction step - what Week 9 calls 'a workflow with an AI step'. In System B the model chooses each lookup, reads what comes back and decides again until its stop rule. The morning schedule is only the trigger, and both systems have one.
questions.trap: A ('Both are agentic because a schedule starts them automatically'). Both systems start without a person, so 'both agentic' is tempting. A schedule is only a trigger: it says when a run starts, not who chooses the steps inside it.
questions.tip: The Week 9 test is 'Who chooses the next step?' A person's flowchart = a workflow (maybe with an AI step). The model choosing, reading results and deciding again = an agent.
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 9 Lecture, slides 7 and 8 (who chooses the next step; when is 'agent' only a label?); LECTURE Week 7 Lecture, slide 8 (the Monday campaign report is a fixed workflow); AIS Week 7 AIS (Zapier), slide 12 (fixed steps or a chosen step); READING Week 10 Lecture, slides 9 to 12 and 24, for revision (a goal, tools, a loop and a stop; who chooses while we are away).

questions.stem: Read the two agent cards below. Using the Week 9 AI product map, where do X and Y sit? Card X: starts every weekday at 07:00; permitted work: read public prices and report to its owner only. Card Y: starts every weekday at 07:00; permitted work: read public prices and update the shared price register.
options: X in Monitor; Y in Autopilot.
X in Autopilot; Y in Monitor.
Both in Ask because a manager receives their reports.
X in Ask; Y in Delegate.
why: ✓ 'X sits in Monitor and Y sits in Autopilot.'
✗ 'This swaps the two cards. Both start on a clock, and only Y changes anything.'
✗ 'Ask needs a person to start each run. Who receives the report does not set the region; the trigger and the permissions do.'
✗ 'Neither card is started by a person, so neither can sit in the left half of the map, where Ask and Delegate are.'
questions.explanation: The Week 9 map is drawn by Q1 (Who starts a run?) and Q3 (What can it touch?). Both cards start on a clock, so both sit on the right half. X only reads and reports to its owner, so it stays low in Monitor ('it starts itself; it reads and reports'). Y updates a shared register that others rely on - it changes things beyond its reply - so it rises into Autopilot ('it starts itself; it changes things'), where the gate moves to before the action.
questions.trap: C ('Both in Ask because a manager receives their reports'). Both cards report to a manager, so 'Ask' looks plausible. But Ask needs a person to start each run; who receives the report does not set the region.
questions.tip: Read Q1 (Who starts a run?) from the trigger and Q3 (What can it touch?) from the permissions. Clock + reads only = Monitor; clock + changes a shared record = Autopilot.
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 9 Lecture, slide 15 (who starts a run, and what can it touch?); LECTURE Week 9 Lecture, slide 31, checkpoint question 1 (a Monday news summary that only reports sits in Monitor); PROBLEM SET Problem Set 7 guide, Runs 4a and 4b (the same scheduled task moved from Monitor to Autopilot); READING Week 10 Lecture, slide 26, for revision (each product moves when we change a setting).

questions.stem: A global purchasing team must enter approved orders into a supplier portal. The portal has no API or connector, and the job requires clicking through forms. Which agent family is the closest fit, with approval before submission?
options: Builders and frameworks, regardless of the task.
Answer and research.
Coding and app building.
Browser and computer use.
why: ✗ 'Builders and frameworks let you build your own agent. Picking a family regardless of the task breaks the rule to start from the job.'
✗ 'Answer and research reads and replies with sources. It cannot click through forms.'
✗ 'Coding and app building writes and ships code. With no API to code against, the job is clicking through screens.'
✓ 'Browser and computer use is the closest family, with approval set before the agent submits.'
questions.explanation: Family 2, Browser and computer use, 'clicks, types and fills in forms on a website or screen', and Week 9 said a browser agent fits sites with no API and no connector. You start the agent and it acts in a browser, which places it in Delegate on the Week 9 map ('you start it; it changes things'); the approval before submission is its gate - the rule to stop before it buys, books, submits or sends.
questions.trap: C ('Coding and app building'). Entering orders into a portal sounds like a technical job. But with no API to code against, the work is clicking through screens.
questions.tip: Start from the job, then pick the family and the gate. No API + no connector + clicking forms = Browser and computer use (family 2), Delegate, approval before submit.
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 9 Lecture, slides 17 and 18 (the families by job; a browser agent fits sites with no API and no connector); LECTURE Week 9 Lecture, slides 23 and 26 (start from the job; when is an agent the wrong tool?); AIS Week 9 AIS, slides 7 and 14 (stop before it buys, books, submits or sends; where a browser agent's gate sits); PROBLEM SET Problem Set 7 guide, Run 2 (Claude in Chrome with Manually approve).

questions.stem: A manager starts a research assistant herself. It reads public sources for twenty minutes and returns a brief. It cannot write files, change records or act in an account. Where does it sit on the Week 9 AI product map?
options: Autopilot, because it works for twenty minutes.
Delegate, because the manager gave it a substantial job.
Monitor, because it reads the web.
Ask, because the manager starts it and it only reads and replies.
why: ✗ 'Autopilot needs a run that starts itself and changes things. How long it runs sets the dot size, and the region stays the same.'
✗ 'A substantial job is not the test for Delegate. Delegate needs the agent to change things beyond its reply.'
✗ 'Monitor needs a schedule, an event or the agent itself to start the run. Reading the web keeps it low, in Ask or Monitor.'
✓ It sits in Ask because the manager starts it and it only reads and replies.
questions.explanation: The map is drawn by Q1 (Who starts a run?) and Q3 (What can it touch?). The manager starts the run herself (left half), and it only reads public sources and returns a brief (bottom row) - so Ask ('you start it; it reads and replies'). Twenty minutes answers Q2 (How long does one run go on?), which the map shows only as dot size. The studio's research station sat in Ask for the same reason.
questions.trap: C ('Monitor, because it reads the web'). It reads the web, so 'Monitor' sounds right. But Monitor needs a schedule, an event or the agent itself to start the run; here the manager starts it.
questions.tip: How long it runs is Q2 (How long does one run go on its own?), shown only as dot size. Region = Q1 (Who starts a run?) + Q3 (What can it touch?). Manager starts + reads and replies = Ask.
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 9 Lecture, slide 15 (Ask, and dot size shows Q2, how long it runs); LECTURE Week 9 Lecture, slide 10 (what to ask of any agent product, Q1 to Q6); AIS Week 9 AIS, slides 4 and 17 (a research run of 5 to 15 minutes sits in Ask); PROBLEM SET Problem Set 7 guide, Run 1 (Claude chat with your two files placed dot 1 in Ask).

questions.stem: A multinational retailer's operations team believes late deliveries should always be escalated to a regional manager. It assumes the customer-service team takes the same position. When asked independently, the customer-service team says routine delays should be handled locally. What does this show about the operations team's congruency and accuracy?
options: Its congruency is low, but its accuracy is high because the teams disagree.
Its congruency is high, but its accuracy is low: it expects agreement and misreads the other team.
Its congruency and accuracy are both high because it has a clear policy.
Its accuracy is high because its estimate matches its own position.
why: ✗ 'This swaps the two measures. The team's estimate matches its own view, so its congruency is high; the teams disagreeing is low agreement.'
✓ 'The operations team's congruency is high and its accuracy is low: it expects agreement and misreads customer service.'
✗ 'A clear policy is only the team's own view. Accuracy needs the estimate to match what customer service said, and it does not.'
✗ 'An estimate that matches your own position is the definition of congruency. Accuracy is checked against the other team's actual answer.'
questions.explanation: Congruency compares a team's own view (E, my own answer) with its own estimate of the other team (F, my estimate of the other side); accuracy compares that estimate (F) with the other team's actual view (G, the other side's actual answer). Operations wants escalation and assumes customer service agrees, so E = F: high congruency. Customer service actually prefers local handling, so F does not equal G: low accuracy. Side A in the F7 example did the same.
questions.trap: A ('Its congruency is low, but its accuracy is high because the teams disagree'). It swaps the two measures. The team's estimate matches its own view, so congruency is HIGH; the teams disagreeing is low AGREEMENT, not high accuracy.
questions.tip: Write E, F, G before answering. Congruency = E (my own answer) vs F (my estimate of the other side). Accuracy = F vs G (the other side's actual answer).

questions.stem: Two regional teams and their AI agents are building one customer-support service. Both teams read the same version of SPEC.md. Team A believes every refund needs a person's approval. Team B believes refunds below EUR 50 may be issued automatically. Asked separately, each team says the other team follows its own rule. No external answer key has yet settled which rule should apply. Which state best describes the relationship between the teams?
options: False conflict: their views agree, but each believes they differ.
False consensus: their views differ, but each believes they agree.
Shared error: both hold the same view, and an answer key shows it is wrong.
Dissensus: their views differ, and both recognise the difference.
why: ✗ 'False conflict needs the views to agree while someone thinks they differ. Here the views differ.'
✓ 'The teams are in false consensus: their views differ, and each believes they agree.'
✗ 'Shared error needs the same view on both sides and an answer key that shows it is wrong. Neither holds here.'
✗ 'Dissensus needs both teams to see the difference. Here each team believes the other agrees with it.'
questions.explanation: The four states cross two questions: do the teams agree, and does each see where they stand? Team A (person approves every refund) and Team B (under EUR 50 automatic) disagree, yet each says the other follows its own rule, so each expects agreement and misreads the other - false consensus (the PS6 'Hidden gap'; action: check the key). Both read the same SPEC.md and no answer key has ruled, so neither a version gap nor shared error explains it.
questions.trap: D ('Dissensus: their views differ, and both recognise the difference'). The teams do disagree, so 'dissensus' is tempting. But dissensus needs both teams to SEE the difference; here each believes the other agrees.
questions.tip: Two questions: Do they agree? Does each see where they stand? Disagree + each thinks they agree = false consensus (the 'hidden gap'; action: check the key).
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Co-Collaboration Model deck, slide 8 (what happens when we cross agreement with perceived agreement?); slides 14 and 15 (deciding the state; the treasury desk's word 'moves'); slide 20 (views that rest on different SPEC.md versions); RESULTS PS6 results for students, slides 3 to 8 (the hidden gap and the other presets).

questions.stem: Finance and Sales both hold that a discount above 15% needs the CFO's approval. Asked separately, Finance says Sales wants reps to approve any discount themselves, and Sales says Finance wants every discount sent to the CFO. Define congruency and accuracy, name the state the two teams are in, and say what should happen next.

parts.label: (a)
parts.task: Define congruency and accuracy.
parts.model: Congruency compares a team's own view with its estimate of the other team's view. Accuracy compares a team's estimate with the other team's actual view. Agreement compares the two teams' own views.

parts.label: (b)
parts.task: Explain how the measures name the state.
parts.model: Read together, the three measures name the state: consensus, dissensus, false consensus or false conflict. False conflict means the teams agree, but one or both think they disagree.

parts.label: (c)
parts.task: Name the state of Finance and Sales.
parts.model: Their own views match, so agreement is high. Each team expects disagreement, so its congruency is low, and each misreads the other, so its accuracy is low. The state is false conflict.

parts.label: (d)
parts.task: Say what should happen next.
parts.model: Show both teams each other's actual answers. Then write the shared rule into the one document both teams work from, with a test case, such as a 16% discount that must go to the CFO.

questions.modelAnswer: (a) Congruency compares a team's own view with its estimate of the other team's view. Accuracy compares a team's estimate with the other team's actual view. Agreement compares the two teams' own views. (b) Read together, the three measures name the state: consensus, dissensus, false consensus or false conflict. False conflict means the teams agree, but one or both think they disagree. (c) Their own views match, so agreement is high. Each team expects disagreement, so its congruency is low, and each misreads the other, so its accuracy is low. The state is false conflict. (d) Show both teams each other's actual answers. Then write the shared rule into the one document both teams work from, with a test case, such as a 16% discount that must go to the CFO.
questions.explanation: Define: congruency as own view against own estimate, and accuracy as estimate against the other team's actual view. Explain: agreement, read with what each team believes about the other, names the state. Apply: the views match while both teams expect disagreement and misread each other, so the state is false conflict. Check: each team should see the other's answers, and the shared rule and a test case go into the shared document.
questions.trap: Calling it disagreement. The teams agree; what is wrong is what each believes about the other.
questions.tip: Five states (p.144): consensus, dissensus, false consensus, false conflict, shared error.
questions.source: Where we met it: Lecture: The Human-AI Co-Collaboration Model, slides 6 to 8 and 14; Results: Problem Set 6 results, shown in Week 9, slides 2 to 4; Quiz 4, Questions 1 and 4

questions.stem: A consumer-goods company compares two products built on the same model. One answers questions from uploaded files. The other can run overnight, update records and retain files between runs. What best explains the difference?
options: The second product must have more parameters.
The first product must use an older training dataset.
Their harnesses provide different triggers, permissions, memory and control flow.
Identical models must behave identically in every product.
why: ✗ 'The stem says both use the same model. More parameters would not give a product a clock or permission to update records.'
✗ 'Training data shapes what a model learned. It does not decide whether a product starts overnight or updates records.'
✓ 'Their harnesses give them different triggers, permissions, memory and control flow.'
✗ 'The same model sits inside different harnesses here, so the products behave differently. This option contradicts the Week 9 rule.'
questions.explanation: The harness is everything around the model: instructions, tools, memory, control flow, validation and permissions, with a trigger that starts each run and a gate where a person approves. The file-answering product waits for you, reads what you upload and stops after one reply; the overnight product has a clock, permission to update records, files kept between runs and a loop. As Week 9 put it, the same model in a different harness makes a different product.
questions.trap: A ('The second product must have more parameters'). 'Bigger model = more capable product' is a common belief. But the stem says the same model; parameters cannot give a product a clock or permission to update records.
questions.tip: Same model, different behaviour = different harness (trigger, permissions, memory, control flow). Compare harnesses first, then the models inside them.
questions.source: Where we met it: LECTURE Week 9 Lecture, slide 6 (same model, different harness, different product); LECTURE Week 9 Lecture, slides 5 and 11 (a model in a loop, inside a harness; each product across Q1 to Q6); PROBLEM SET Problem Set 7, section D (the model stays much the same while the harness around it changes); READING Week 10 Lecture, slides 17, 18 and 47, for revision (what the harness decides).

questions.official: Part B Practice 5 — The harness and the map
questions.stem: A procurement manager sets up a Claude scheduled task for every Friday at 9:00 AM. It reads the purchase-order sheet, drafts a reminder to each supplier whose delivery is late, and sends it from the team's mailbox. Define the harness, place the task on the Week 9 map with Q1 (Who starts a run?) and Q3 (What can it touch?), and say where the gate must sit and who answers for the emails.

parts.label: (a)
parts.task: Define the harness.
parts.model: A harness is everything around the model: what it reads, the tools it may call, where it runs, the gate that decides each action and the record of what it did. The model only writes the next step.

parts.label: (b)
parts.task: Explain how Q1 (Who starts a run?) and Q3 (What can it touch?) are read.
parts.model: Q1 asks who starts a run, and Q3 what it can touch. The settings of the harness answer both, because a prompt can only ask.

parts.label: (c)
parts.task: Place the task on the Week 9 map.
parts.model: A schedule starts it, so it sits on the right of the map. It sends email to suppliers, which changes things beyond its reply, so it sits at the top. The task is in Autopilot.

parts.label: (d)
parts.task: Say where the gate must sit and who answers for the emails.
parts.model: In Autopilot the gate moves to before the action. Let the task save Gmail drafts only, or remove the send tool, so a person approves each email, and read the run history every Friday. The manager who set it up answers for what it sends.

questions.modelAnswer: (a) A harness is everything around the model: what it reads, the tools it may call, where it runs, the gate that decides each action and the record of what it did. The model only writes the next step. (b) Q1 asks who starts a run, and Q3 what it can touch. The settings of the harness answer both, because a prompt can only ask. (c) A schedule starts it, so it sits on the right of the map. It sends email to suppliers, which changes things beyond its reply, so it sits at the top. The task is in Autopilot. (d) In Autopilot the gate moves to before the action. Let the task save Gmail drafts only, or remove the send tool, so a person approves each email, and read the run history every Friday. The manager who set it up answers for what it sends.
keywords: the gate moves to before the action
questions.explanation: Define: the harness as everything around the model, which only writes the next step. Explain: Q1 and Q3 are read from the settings, because a prompt can only ask. Apply: place the task in Autopilot, because a schedule starts it and it sends email beyond its reply. Check: put the gate before sending, with drafts only or no send tool, read the Friday run history, and name the manager as the one who answers.
questions.trap: Writing 'tell it in the prompt not to send'. A sentence in the prompt cannot take back what the send tool allows.
questions.tip: This is the pack's only Part B question drawing on the Week 10 harness lecture (slide 47). Map axes: Q1 (horizontal) who starts a run: you, each time -> a schedule, an event or itself; Q3 (vertical) reads only -> changes things. Quadrants: Ask (bottom-left), Monitor (bottom-right), Delegate (top-left), Autopilot (top-right).

questions.official: Studio checkpoint 2 — Stitch to an API (Revision Pack p.113)
questions.stem: You changed the screen in Google AI Studio an hour ago. The Vercel URL still shows the old screen, and the last deployment is green. What is the most likely cause?
options: The change was never pushed
Vercel needs Redeploy after each edit
The URL needs a hash in it
The short URL keeps the first build
why: ✓ editing in Google AI Studio sends nothing anywhere. Vercel builds from GitHub, so nothing changes until a push arrives.
✗ every push to main redeploys automatically; no manual Redeploy is needed after each edit.
✗ a URL with a hash is a preview that asks visitors to sign in; it does not fix a missing push.
✗ the short URL always serves the latest production build.
questions.explanation: A green last deployment means the last push built fine. The edit made an hour ago in AI Studio was never pushed, so GitHub and Vercel never saw it. A step is done only when you see its result at the destination. (Prof Roh: Editing in AI Studio sends nothing anywhere, and Vercel builds from GitHub, so nothing changes until a push arrives. Problem Set 1, step B2.)
questions.trap: 'Vercel needs Redeploy after each edit' sounds like the Checkpoint 1 lesson. But that rule is for environment variables; code changes deploy on every push.
questions.tip: Name the station first. AI Studio (build) hands code to GitHub (keep) only when you push; Vercel (host) builds from GitHub. Check the commit time on github.com.
questions.source: Where we met it: Revision Pack p.113, checkpoint 'Stitch to an API'

questions.official: Studio checkpoint 3 — Stitch to an API (Revision Pack p.113)
questions.stem: A Problem Set 1 page is blank on Vercel. You add GEMINI_API_KEY there and redeploy, and the page loads. What have you done?
options: Fixed it as the brief asks
Published the key to every visitor
Kept the key on the server
Made the repository private
why: ✗ the brief asks you to remove the Gemini code, not to supply its key.
✓ the vite.config.ts line writes GEMINI_API_KEY into the JavaScript every visitor downloads, so the key is now public.
✗ this key is not kept on the server; the config line puts it in the front end.
✗ making the repository private changes nothing about the JavaScript served to visitors.
questions.explanation: The page loaded, so it looks fixed. But the config line copies the key into the browser bundle, so every visitor can read it with View Source. The right repair was to remove the @google/genai import, its client and the key handling. (Prof Roh: The vite.config.ts line puts the key in the JavaScript every visitor downloads. The brief asks you to remove the Gemini code. Problem Set 1, section 3.)
questions.trap: 'Kept the key on the server' is tempting because Vercel feels like 'the server'. But the build writes the key into the downloadable JavaScript.
questions.tip: Blank white page + green build in PS1 = remove the Gemini code ('Change nothing else'), push again. Never cure it by adding GEMINI_API_KEY.
questions.source: Where we met it: Revision Pack p.113, checkpoint 'Stitch to an API'

questions.official: Studio checkpoint 1 — Stitch to an API (Revision Pack p.113)
questions.stem: A group saved LTA_ACCOUNT_KEY in Vercel and opened the app at once. Every call fails with 401, and /api/health shows keyConfigured: false. What should they do first?
options: Re-copy the key from the email
Redeploy the site
Rename it VITE_LTA_ACCOUNT_KEY
Rewrite the BusArrival address
why: ✗ re-copying helps when LTA answers 401 with keyConfigured true. Here the key never reached the running site.
✓ a saved variable reaches only a build that starts after it. keyConfigured false says the running site never got it, so redeploy, then read /api/health again.
✗ a VITE_ name would write the key into the JavaScript every visitor downloads.
✗ a wrong address gives 404 from LTA, and it cannot explain keyConfigured false.
questions.explanation: Saving a variable in Vercel does not change the site that is already running. Only a build that starts after the save reads it, so the group must Redeploy and then open /api/health to see keyConfigured: true. (Prof Roh: A saved variable reaches only a build that starts after it, and keyConfigured false says the running site never got it. Week 3 AIS, slide 18.)
questions.trap: 'Re-copy the key' is tempting because 401 sounds like a bad key. But /api/health already says keyConfigured: false, so the value never arrived.
questions.tip: Read /api/health first. keyConfigured false = Redeploy. keyConfigured true + 401 = re-copy the key. 404 = check the address character by character.
questions.source: Where we met it: Revision Pack p.113, checkpoint 'Stitch to an API'

questions.official: Studio checkpoint 4 — Stitch to an API (Revision Pack p.113)
questions.stem: Opening /api/bus inside the AI Studio preview returns the text of your function with a 200. What does this tell you?
options: The function ran
The key has leaked
api/ belongs inside src/
Nothing ran; test on Vercel
why: ✗ a 200 here is the file's source returned with a success code; no function ran.
✗ seeing your own function's code is not seeing the key, which lives in Vercel.
✗ api/ must sit at the root beside package.json; inside src/ Vercel builds no function.
✓ the preview does not use Vercel's folder routing, so it returns the source text. Test the function on the Vercel URL.
questions.explanation: Google AI Studio's preview serves files; it does not run Vercel functions. So /api/bus returns the text of api/bus.js with a 200. Only the deployed Vercel URL runs the function where the key lives. (Prof Roh: The preview does not use Vercel's folder routing, so it returns the file's source with a success code. Week 3 AIS, slide 16.)
questions.trap: 'The function ran' is tempting because 200 means success. But the body is the JavaScript source, which shows nothing ran.
questions.tip: Read the body, not only the status code. Source code back = nothing ran. JSON with each service and its next two buses = the function ran on Vercel.
questions.source: Where we met it: Revision Pack p.113, checkpoint 'Stitch to an API'

questions.official: Studio checkpoint 7 — Clarity, Disqus and heuristics (Revision Pack p.131)
questions.stem: A draft privacy notice for your product says "Microsoft Clarity collects anonymous data." What should change?
options: Keep it, since numbers are masked
Drop it, as no notice is needed
Name only Disqus, which shows ads
Call it pseudonymous usage data
why: ✗ masking numbers does not make the data anonymous; a cookie still recognises a returning browser.
✗ Clarity's terms require a privacy notice.
✗ the notice must name both Clarity and Disqus, which sets cookies and shows ads on the free plan.
✓ Problem Set 3 asked you to call it usage data and never anonymous, because a cookie recognises a returning browser, which makes it pseudonymous.
questions.explanation: Microsoft Clarity sets a cookie that recognises a returning browser, so visits can be linked to the same person. That is pseudonymous, not anonymous, and Clarity's terms require a privacy notice that says so. (Prof Roh: Problem Set 3 asked you to describe what Clarity collects as usage data and not to call it anonymous, because a cookie recognises a returning browser, which makes the data pseudonymous. Clarity's terms require the notice.)
questions.trap: 'Keep it, since numbers are masked' is tempting because Clarity masks numbers and emails by default. Masking hides content; the cookie still links visits.
questions.tip: Clarity = pseudonymous usage data, never 'anonymous'. The notice names Clarity and Disqus, with links, in the footer of every page.
questions.source: Where we met it: Revision Pack p.131, checkpoint 'Clarity, Disqus and heuristics'

questions.official: Studio checkpoint 5 — Clarity, Disqus and heuristics (Revision Pack p.130)
questions.stem: Three groupmates reviewed your product, and you have fixed its one severity 4. Which finding do you repair next?
options: Severity 3, raised by one
Severity 3, raised by two
Severity 2, raised by all three
Severity 1, raised by all three
why: ✗ a severity 3 raised by one shares the next tier with a severity 2 raised by all three.
✓ two of three is most, and a severity 3 met by most comes straight after any severity 4.
✗ a severity 2 raised by all three is in the tier after severity 3 raised by most.
✗ a severity 1 is left, with a reason given in your reply.
questions.explanation: Severity comes first and reach second. With the severity 4 fixed, the severity 3 raised by most of the group (two of three) is next. A severity 3 raised by one and a severity 2 raised by all three come after it. (Prof Roh: Two of three groupmates is most, and a severity 3 met by most comes straight after any severity 4. A severity 3 raised by one and a severity 2 raised by all three share the next tier, where the more widely met goes first (Problem Set 4, Step 5).)
questions.trap: 'Severity 2, raised by all three' is tempting because everyone saw it. But severity leads; reach only orders findings inside a tier.
questions.tip: Fix order (PS4 Step 5): severity 4 first, however few meet it; then severity 3 raised by most; then the next tier, widest reach first; severity 1: leave and say why.
questions.source: Where we met it: Revision Pack p.130, checkpoint 'Clarity, Disqus and heuristics'

questions.official: Studio checkpoint 6 — Clarity, Disqus and heuristics (Revision Pack p.130)
questions.stem: Your route sends back the same response when a stop has no buses due and when the transport authority cannot be reached, and the page shows "Something went wrong" for both. Where does the repair belong?
options: System: the route keeps the two apart
System: a longer timeout on the call
Screen: a friendlier sentence
Screen: a retry button
why: ✓ both situations reach the screen as the same response, so the route must keep them apart before the screen can describe either.
✗ a longer timeout still leaves 'no buses due' and 'cannot reach LTA' sharing one response.
✗ no wording can separate two cases the screen cannot tell apart.
✗ a retry button does not tell the person which of the two happened.
questions.explanation: This is Help Users Recognize, Diagnose, and Recover from Errors (heuristic 9) with a system cause. The route must return different responses for 'no buses due' and 'provider unreachable'; only then can the screen say which happened. (Prof Roh: Both situations reach the screen as the same response, so no wording or button on the screen can separate them, and a longer timeout leaves them sharing one response. The route has to keep them apart before the screen can describe either (Week 5 AIS, slide 39).)
questions.trap: 'Screen: a friendlier sentence' is tempting because the symptom is on the screen. But the screen receives identical responses, so it cannot know which case it is.
questions.tip: Screen or system? Ask whether the screen could fix it with what it already receives. If it needs something it is never sent, the repair belongs to the system (the function in api/).
questions.source: Where we met it: Revision Pack p.130, checkpoint 'Clarity, Disqus and heuristics'

questions.official: Studio checkpoint 8 — Clarity, Disqus and heuristics (Revision Pack p.131)
questions.stem: Why did predictions.md have to be pushed before the first comment reached your board?
options: So groupmates could read it first
So its commit time shows what you believed
So your agent could use it
So Disqus could link to it
why: ✗ groupmates were asked NOT to open the file until they had posted.
✓ its commit time shows what you believed at the start, before any finding could change your memory of it (hindsight bias).
✗ the file was a record for you and the reader, not input for your coding agent.
✗ Disqus does not link to it; it holds the findings, not the prediction.
questions.explanation: Once you have read a critical finding you cannot un-read it, and you later recall your own view as closer to it than it was. A commit time before the first comment is the evidence of what you predicted, which keeps you honest against confirmation bias. (Prof Roh: Once you have read a critical finding you cannot un-read it, and you later recall your own evaluation as closer to it than it was. The commit time shows what you believed at the start, and groupmates were asked not to open the file until they had posted (Problem Set 4, Section E and Step 3).)
questions.trap: 'So groupmates could read it first' is tempting because it was public in the repository. But they were asked not to open it until they had posted, so it could not steer them.
questions.tip: predictions.md = a test agreed in advance (adversarial collaboration). Pushed before the first comment, its commit time proves what you believed before seeing any finding.
questions.source: Where we met it: Revision Pack p.131, checkpoint 'Clarity, Disqus and heuristics'

questions.stem: A marketing manager asks a chat model for five published studies on loyalty programmes in Singapore's hawker centres. It returns five well-formatted references with authors, years and journals. Define next-token prediction, explain why the references may not exist, apply it to this request, and say what the manager should do before quoting them.

parts.label: (a)
parts.task: Define next-token prediction.
parts.model: A language model is trained to predict the next token, a piece of text, from the tokens before it. To write a reply it scores every possible next token, picks one, adds it to the text and repeats, so a long answer is many small predictions in a row.

parts.label: (b)
parts.task: Explain why the references may not exist.
parts.model: Nothing in that process looks anything up or checks it. A reference with authors, a year and a journal is plausible text, so the model can write one for a study that does not exist, and how confident it sounds tells us nothing about whether it is right.

parts.label: (c)
parts.task: Apply it to this request.
parts.model: Loyalty programmes in Singapore's hawker centres are a niche, local topic that the training text barely covered, which is where made-up answers gather. So all five references are at high risk, however well they are formatted.

parts.label: (d)
parts.task: Say what the manager should check or do.
parts.model: Before quoting any of them, she opens each study herself in a library database or on the publisher's site, confirms the authors, year and finding, and drops any she cannot find. She records the link she opened beside each citation.

To write a reply it scores every possible next token, picks one, adds it to the text and repeats, so a long answer is many small predictions in a row. (b) Nothing in that process looks anything up or checks it. A reference with authors, a year and a journal is plausible text, so the model can write one for a study that does not exist, and how confident it sounds tells us nothing about whether it is right. (c) Loyalty programmes in Singapore's hawker centres are a niche, local topic that the training text barely covered, which is where made-up answers gather. So all five references are at high risk, however well they are formatted. (d) Before quoting any of them, she opens each study herself in a library database or on the publisher's site, confirms the authors, year and finding, and drops any she cannot find. She records the link she opened beside each citation.
questions.explanation: One point for each part. (a) Define: A language model is trained to predict the next token, a piece of text, from the tokens before it. (b) Explain: Nothing in that process looks anything up or checks it. (c) Apply: Loyalty programmes in Singapore's hawker centres are a niche, local topic that the training text barely covered, which is where made-up answers gather. (d) Check: Before quoting any of them, she opens each study herself in a library database or on the publisher's site, confirms the authors, year and finding, and drops any she cannot find.
questions.trap: Writing 'the model searched badly' or 'the AI lied'. It searched nothing and has no intent; it wrote plausible next tokens.
questions.tip: Made-up answers live where training text is thin: niche, recent, local, private. Your Check is always 'open the source yourself'.

questions.stem: A bank's customer chatbot gives slightly different answers on different days when customers ask the same question about overdraft fees. Compliance wants the same approved answer every time. Define decoding and temperature, explain why answers vary, choose the setting for the fee answer, and say what compliance should still check.

parts.label: (a)
parts.task: Define decoding and temperature.
parts.model: After a prompt the model holds a probability for every candidate next token. Decoding is the step that picks one: greedy decoding always takes the most likely token, and sampling draws from the spread like a weighted die. Temperature reshapes the spread before the draw.

parts.label: (b)
parts.task: Explain why the answers vary.
parts.model: At temperature 0 the pick is greedy, so the same prompt gives the same answer every run (deterministic). Higher temperatures flatten the spread, so less likely tokens are picked more often and runs differ (stochastic). Temperature changes the picking, not what the model learned.

parts.label: (c)
parts.task: Choose the setting for the fee answer.
parts.model: The chatbot samples at a moderate temperature, so the same question can take a different token at some step and drift into a different answer. For the fee answer the bank sets temperature at or near 0 and puts the approved fee text in the model's context.

parts.label: (d)
parts.task: Say what compliance should check.
parts.model: Compliance compares the answer with the approved fee schedule before release, and again whenever fees change, because a low temperature makes an answer repeatable, not correct: a wrong answer at 0 is repeated every time.

Higher temperatures flatten the spread, so less likely tokens are picked more often and runs differ (stochastic). Temperature changes the picking, not what the model learned. (c) The chatbot samples at a moderate temperature, so the same question can take a different token at some step and drift into a different answer. For the fee answer the bank sets temperature at or near 0 and puts the approved fee text in the model's context. (d) Compliance compares the answer with the approved fee schedule before release, and again whenever fees change, because a low temperature makes an answer repeatable, not correct: a wrong answer at 0 is repeated every time.

questions.stem: A law firm licenses a base model that only continues text. Its plan: (1) associates write model answers to 2,000 typical client questions and the model is trained on them; (2) partners rank several model answers per question from best to worst, and a second model learns that ranking; (3) the second model scores new answers while the first model is nudged toward high scores. Define the three-step process, explain what the reward model is, name each step of the plan, and say what the firm should check.

parts.label: (a)
parts.task: Define the three-step process.
parts.model: Instruction tuning turns a base model that continues text into an assistant in three steps: Step 1, supervised fine-tuning, where people write answers and the model learns to imitate them; Step 2, where people rank the model's answers and a reward model learns the ranking; Step 3, reinforcement learning, where the reward model scores new answers and the model is nudged toward high scores with no person reading each one.

parts.label: (b)
parts.task: Explain what the reward model is.
parts.model: The reward model is a stand-in judge: a second model trained to reproduce people's rankings, so it can score any new answer. Human effort falls at each step, and Steps 2 and 3 together are called RLHF; but the judge rewards what read well to the rankers, and nothing in the loop rewards being right.

parts.label: (c)
parts.task: Name each step of the firm's plan.
parts.model: Plan (1), associates writing answers, is Step 1, supervised fine-tuning. Plan (2), partners ranking answers so a second model learns the order, builds the reward model in Step 2. Plan (3), that judge scoring new answers while the first model is nudged, is Step 3, reinforcement learning.

parts.label: (d)
parts.task: Say what the firm should check.
parts.model: Because nothing in the loop rewards being right, the firm tests the tuned model on questions with known answers, such as settled points of law, before clients use it, and a lawyer still checks every case and statute it cites against the source.

questions.stem: A group's bus app shows an empty list. They open /api/health and read keyConfigured: true, and LTA answered with httpCode 401. What should they do next?
options: Redeploy the site so the saved variable reaches the running build
Read the BusArrival address one character at a time against the docs
Re-copy the key from the LTA email and look for a trailing space
Print the real response and compare its field names with the screen
questions.explanation: Each /api/health reading points to one fix. keyConfigured: true means a value reached the running site, and 401 means LTA refused that value, so the key itself is wrong (often a trailing space). keyConfigured: false would call for a Redeploy; a 404 would call for checking the address; a 200 with an empty screen would call for comparing field names.
questions.trap: A. 'Redeploy' is the fix for keyConfigured: false (Checkpoint 1). Here the key did arrive; LTA just refused it.
questions.tip: Learn the four readings: false = Redeploy; true + 401 = re-copy the key; 404 = check the address; 200 + empty screen = compare field names.
questions.source: Where we met it: Week 3 AIS, slides 20, 21 and 27; Problem Set 2, section 14 ('When it breaks' table in the Revision Pack)

questions.stem: A start-up's dashboard calls a paid weather API that needs a secret key. A developer saved the key as VITE_WEATHER_KEY, and the page calls the API straight from the browser. Define the front end, the back end and an API key, explain the risk, say where the key should go, and what to check.

parts.label: (a)
parts.task: Define the front end, the back end and an API key.
parts.model: The front end is what runs in the visitor's browser: the page and its downloaded JavaScript, all of which anyone can read with View Source. The back end runs on machines we control, such as a serverless function on Vercel. An API key is a secret that tells the provider a request is ours.

parts.label: (b)
parts.task: Explain the risk.
parts.model: A VITE_ variable is written into the JavaScript at build time, so every visitor downloads the key. Whoever copies it can use our quota, run up our bill and act in our name, and bots scan public code for keys within minutes.

parts.label: (c)
parts.task: Apply: say where the key should go.
parts.model: Move the call to the back end. The page calls our own address, such as /api/weather; a function in the api folder reads the key from a server-side environment variable saved in Vercel as a Secret, adds it to the request and returns only the data. The key's name never begins with VITE_, and because it has been published, we rotate it first and tidy second.

parts.label: (d)
parts.task: Say what to check.
parts.model: After saving the new variable, redeploy and open /api/health to see keyConfigured true and the upstream status. Then search the site's JavaScript in the browser for the old key to confirm it is gone, and check the provider's usage page for calls we did not make.

questions.stem: A bus app's Microsoft Clarity shows four taps on the stop name within two seconds in many recordings. Its Disqus board has one comment: 'The stop name looks like a link, but nothing happens when I tap it.' What does each source add?
options: Clarity shows why visitors struggled; Disqus shows how many of them did
Clarity shows where and how often it happens; the comment says why
Both show every visitor's experience, so the two counts can be added up
The comment proves severity 4, because a visitor took the time to write
questions.explanation: The repeated taps are a rage click (the same spot clicked again and again) recorded by Clarity: it shows where and how often. The Disqus comment gives the reason in the visitor's own words, but only the few who choose to write ever do. A heuristic evaluation would then name the heuristic (here Consistency and Standards: only what opens something should look like a link).
questions.trap: A. The first wrong option swaps the two sources. Recordings never tell you why; comments never tell you how often.
questions.tip: Three sources, three jobs: Clarity = what they do (where, how often); Disqus = what a few choose to say (why); heuristic evaluation = what reviewers predict, with the heuristic named.
questions.source: Where we met it: Revision Pack, 'Three sources' (p.116); Problem Set 3; Week 5 AIS

questions.stem: A café-finder app has two comments on its Disqus board, both praising the colours. Microsoft Clarity shows, in many recordings, a dead click on a photo at 0:15, a rage click of five taps at 0:18, and visitors leaving by 0:44. The founder concludes users are happy. Define what Clarity and Disqus each record, explain why they can disagree, apply this to the case, and say what to check.

parts.label: (a)
parts.task: Define what Clarity and Disqus each record.
parts.model: Microsoft Clarity records what visitors do: a recording of each visit, heatmaps of clicks and scrolling, and flags such as a rage click (the same spot clicked again and again) and a dead click (a click on something that does not respond). Disqus records what visitors choose to say, in their own words, in one comment thread.

parts.label: (b)
parts.task: Explain why they can disagree.
parts.model: Each source misses what the other catches: Clarity shows where and how often people struggle but not why, and comments come only from the few who choose to write. Most people who struggle close the tab without a word, so a board of praise says nothing about the silent ones.

parts.label: (c)
parts.task: Apply it to the case.
parts.model: The dead click and the five-tap rage click show many visitors expect the photos to open, and leaving by 0:44 suggests they give up. Two comments cannot outweigh that; the founder is reading only the evidence that fits his belief, which is confirmation bias. A likely finding is Consistency and Standards (heuristic 4): the photos look clickable but do nothing.

parts.label: (d)
parts.task: Say what to check.
parts.model: Open Disqus's Pending and Spam tabs for held comments, watch several recordings of visitors who left early, repair the photo behaviour and compare the rage-click count before and after. The privacy notice should call Clarity's data pseudonymous usage data, never anonymous.

questions.stem: A product team plans a heuristic evaluation of its new booking screen with three reviewers. How should the inspection be run?
options: Each reviewer inspects alone in two passes, then the lists are pooled and all rate the merged list
The three reviewers walk through together so they agree on each finding as they go
One senior reviewer rates every finding, because one careful rating is enough
Watch three real customers try to book, then label each problem with a heuristic
questions.explanation: Reviewers work alone first, with no discussion: a first pass to learn the flow, a second against Nielsen's ten heuristics, one finding per problem. Only then are the lists pooled, and every reviewer rates the whole merged list on the 0 to 4 severity scale; the mean of three ratings is used. One reviewer finds roughly a third of the problems, which is why several work alone.
questions.trap: B. Walking through together feels efficient, but reviewers who talk find the same problems; working alone is what widens coverage.
questions.tip: Heuristic evaluation = 3 to 5 reviewers, alone first, two passes, merged list, mean of three ratings. Watching real people do a task is usability testing, a different method.
questions.source: Where we met it: Revision Pack, 'The method' (pp.121-125); Week 5 AIS; Problem Set 4

questions.stem: A COO says a new AI writing tool gets reports in on time, because 45 tool users filed on time last month. The full table: tool users, 45 on time and 15 late; non-users, 30 on time and 10 late. Define confirmation bias, read the table, and say what the COO should check before rolling the tool out.

parts.label: (a)
parts.task: Define confirmation bias.
parts.model: Confirmation bias is our habit of looking for the cases that agree with what we already believe, and seldom for the ones that could prove us wrong.

parts.label: (b)
parts.task: Explain the confirmation vs falsification method.
parts.model: Counting the agreeing cell, 45 tool users on time, is the confirmation method. The falsification method asks what would prove the belief wrong, non-users filing on time just as often, and compares the on-time rate in each row using all four cells.

parts.label: (c)
parts.task: Read (apply to) the table.
parts.model: Tool users: 45 of 60 = 75%. Non-users: 30 of 40 = 75%. The rates are the same, so the table shows no association between the tool and on-time reports. The cross-products agree: 45 × 10 = 450 and 15 × 30 = 450.

parts.label: (d)
parts.task: Say what the COO should check before rolling it out.
parts.model: The COO should not credit the tool with punctuality on this evidence. If on-time filing is the goal, he can test it, for example by giving the tool to a random half of teams and comparing their on-time rates next quarter, and look at what else drives late reports.

questions.stem: Three groupmates evaluated your bus app. Findings: (A) typing a stop code that does not exist leaves the results area blank, raised by 3 of 3, severity 3; (B) deleting a saved stop has no undo, raised by 1 of 3, severity 4; (C) arrival times appear in two formats, raised by 2 of 3, severity 2. Define heuristic evaluation, explain how severity is set, decide the fix order with each heuristic named, and say what you check after each repair.

parts.label: (a)
parts.task: Define heuristic evaluation.
parts.model: A heuristic evaluation is an inspection in which three to five reviewers, each working alone, check a product against Nielsen's ten heuristics. It predicts problems; watching real people attempt a task is usability testing.

parts.label: (b)
parts.task: Explain how severity is set.
parts.model: Each reviewer makes two passes, first to learn the flow and then against the ten, logging one finding per problem; the lists are pooled and every reviewer rates the merged list. Severity runs from 0 (no problem) to 4 (catastrophe, fix before release), weighing frequency, impact, persistence and market impact, and the mean of three ratings is used.

parts.label: (c)
parts.task: Apply: decide the fix order and name each heuristic.
parts.model: First (B), User Control and Freedom (heuristic 3, a way back from a mistake): a severity 4 comes first however few meet it. Next (A), Help Users Recognize, Diagnose, and Recover from Errors (heuristic 9), a severity 3 raised by all three; it is a system repair, because the route must report a stop code that does not exist differently from a stop with no buses due. Then (C), Consistency and Standards (heuristic 4), as time allows.

parts.label: (d)
parts.task: Say what you check after each repair.
parts.model: Commit each repair separately, walk the finding again on the live address on a phone, and reply on the Disqus board so the groupmate who raised it can try it. With three reviewers, report counts, never percentages.

questions.stem: Match each of Nielsen's ten heuristics to the question it asks.

pairs.right: Does the person know what is happening right now?

pairs.left: 2 Match Between the System and the Real World
pairs.right: Are the words theirs, or the database's?
Is there a way back from a mistake?
Does the same thing always look and behave the same way?
Could the mistake have been made impossible?
Can they see the options, or must they remember them?
Is there a faster path for the person who comes every day?
Does anything on screen compete with the answer?

pairs.left: 9 Help Users Recognize, Diagnose, and Recover from Errors

questions.explanation: Learn each heuristic by its question; in the exam, read the case, ask each question, and pick the one the case breaks. Codes from a database break 2; one thing written in different ways breaks 4.

questions.stem: An insurer's claims agent writes the text: pay_claim {"claim": 88, "amount": 4000}. The firm wants any payment above S$1,000 refused unless a person approves it. Using Week 5's four boxes of a tool call, where must that refusal live?
options: Box 1, in the model's instructions, so it never writes such a call
Box 3, inside the payment tool, once the transfer has been made
Box 4, in the result the model reads, so it can correct itself
Box 2, where the firm's harness reads the call before any tool runs
questions.explanation: Week 5: '1 the model writes · 2 your harness reads · 3 the tool runs · 4 the result comes back.' 'Nothing in box 1 is an action. It is a sentence asking for one.' Box 2 is the firm's own software, 'the only place a refusal can live'. A rule written into box 1 is only a request the model reads.
questions.trap: A. Box 1 is tempting because instructions feel like control. But an instruction is a sentence the model reads; it cannot hold a call the harness has allowed.
questions.tip: Whenever a question asks where a rule can actually stop an action, answer with the harness or settings (box 2, a permission, a gate), never the prompt.
questions.source: Where we met it: Week 5 lecture (From Chatbots to Agents), the four boxes of a tool call

questions.stem: A procurement agent reads 40 supplier quote files and then sends one acceptance email to the winning supplier. Which of Week 5's dimensions of autonomy says that one step needs the most care?
options: Scope: how many files and systems it reads in one run
Authority: may it read, draft, send or spend?
Duration: how long the run goes on before something stops it
Choice: how many different paths it can pick between
questions.explanation: Week 5 described autonomy along four dimensions: choice, duration, scope and authority. 'One step that sends the acceptance email carries more authority than all forty' reads. 'The level is set by the step with the most authority, here the send.' So the send is where the gate belongs.
questions.trap: A. Scope is tempting because 40 files sounds like a lot. But reading changes nothing; sending commits the firm.
questions.tip: Set the level of an agent by its single most powerful step (send, pay, delete), not by how much it reads.
questions.source: Where we met it: Week 5 lecture, 'How much may it do alone?' (choice, duration, scope, authority)

questions.stem: A procurement team uses AI in two ways: (1) a chatbot drafts a supplier email that the buyer edits and sends; (2) a system reads quote files, checks stock through a supplier's API, chooses another supplier when a stock check fails, and prepares the acceptance email. Define an agent, explain the loop, decide which system is an agent, and say where a person should check.

parts.label: (a)
parts.task: Define an agent.
parts.model: An agent is the same model placed inside a loop, given a short list of tools it may use, and left to keep going until a stop rule ends the run. A chatbot answers once, and the person does everything that follows.

parts.label: (b)
parts.task: Explain how the loop works.
parts.model: In each turn the model writes a tool call as text, the harness reads it and decides whether it may run, the tool runs, and the result returns to the model, which chooses the next step from what came back. Nothing the model writes is an action until the harness lets it run, so the harness is the only place a refusal can live.

parts.label: (c)
parts.task: Apply: decide which system is an agent.
parts.model: System (1) is generative AI in a chatbot: it writes, and the buyer edits and sends. System (2) is an agent: the model chooses another supplier after a failed stock check, so its next step depends on what the last step found, and it keeps calling tools until its stop rule.

parts.label: (d)
parts.task: Say where a person should check.
parts.model: The acceptance email carries the most authority, so the harness holds it as a draft or asks before sending, and a buyer approves it. After each run the buyer reads the record: which quotes it read, which tools it called and why it chose that supplier.

questions.stem: A shared-services manager wants an agent to label supplier invoices in the accounts-payable mailbox every night at 2 AM, when nobody is online. Before it may run unattended, which decisions does Week 6 say she must make?
options: The Instructions field, the Connectors, the Schedule, the wall and the Runs list
The model's size, its temperature, the token limit, the prompt and the vendor
A job in words, a trigger, its tools, its memory and a stop rule
Read, Draft, Act with approval, Act alone, and who reads the record

Memory hook: J-T-T-M-S.
questions.trap: A. The first wrong option uses real course words, but it lists where the parts live in Claude Code, not the decisions you make.
questions.tip: Decisions = Job, Trigger, Tools, Memory, Stop rule (J-T-T-M-S). Places to click = Instructions, Connectors, Schedule, wall, Runs list. Levels = Read, Draft, Act with approval, Act alone.
questions.source: Where we met it: Week 6 lecture, 'An agent that works alone needs five things'

questions.stem: A sales-operations routine runs each morning and emails a list of 'new leads'. Every day it reports the same 40 leads as new. What is the most likely cause?
options: Its temperature is set too low, so it repeats yesterday's answer word for word
Its schedule trigger fires twice, so it reads the lead sheet twice each morning
Its model's training data is out of date, so it cannot tell old leads from new
Each run starts fresh, and nothing records which leads it already reported
questions.explanation: Week 6: 'Each run starts fresh with only the job; anything to remember must be left where it looks.' Memory between runs is something you build: a notes file it reads first and adds to last, an append-only file such as findings.md, or a label it applied last time. Here the routine needs, for example, a file of lead IDs already reported. What it keeps about customers is personal data under the PDPA.
questions.trap: A. Temperature is tempting because the output repeats. But temperature changes how the model picks words, not what it remembers between runs.
questions.tip: A routine that repeats work every run = missing memory. Memory is a file or a label you design, never something the model keeps by itself.
questions.source: Where we met it: Week 6 lecture, 'Memory between runs is something you build'

questions.stem: An overnight reconciliation agent kept calling a bank API that was down. By morning it had retried about 3,000 times and run up a large tool-call bill. What was missing?
options: A stop rule held by the harness: done, stuck after repeated failures, or out of budget
A politer prompt asking the agent to be careful with the firm's money
A stronger model that would have known the bank API was down
A later trigger, so the run started after the bank fixed its API
questions.explanation: Week 6: 'A run has to know how to stop' - done (the job is met), stuck (a tool keeps failing, so it reports and ends), or out of budget (a cap on turns, tool calls or spend 'that the harness holds, whatever the model wants next'). 'A run with no stop rule keeps spending, and keeps reaching whatever its connectors reach.' Example: stop after 50 tool calls or if a tool fails three times in a row, and report which.
questions.trap: B. The politer prompt is a sentence the model reads; a budget cap must sit in the harness, where the model cannot talk past it.
questions.tip: Stop rule = done, stuck, out of budget. People forget it because a chat stops when you stop typing.
questions.source: Where we met it: Week 6 lecture, 'A run has to know how to stop'

questions.stem: A clinic's inbox agent writes replies to patients' questions and saves each as a draft; a nurse reads it and presses send herself. Which of Week 6's four levels is this, and who is exposed if a draft is wrong?
options: Act with approval: the patient, because the nurse only clicks approve
Draft: nobody outside, because a person reads each draft first
Read: only the nurse's time, because the agent itself sends nothing
Act alone: the patient and the clinic, because the agent wrote the words
questions.explanation: Week 6's four levels, set by who is exposed if it is wrong: Read (reports; only your time), Draft (writes replies a person sends; nobody outside, you read the draft first), Act with approval (asks before each send, then the agent sends once you allow it; you and the recipient), Act alone (sends without asking; the recipient, your firm and you afterwards). Here the nurse sends, so it is Draft.
questions.trap: A. Act with approval is tempting because a person clicks. But at that level the agent sends once you allow it; at Draft the person does the sending.
questions.tip: Ask 'who presses send?' The person = Draft. The agent after you allow = Act with approval. The agent without asking = Act alone.
questions.source: Where we met it: Week 6 lecture, 'How much may the inbox agent do?'

questions.stem: An inbox routine's Instructions say 'never delete mail'. Week 6 assumed a 1% chance per action that such a rule slips, and a check-in every 200 actions. What did the deck work out, and what is the fix?
options: About a 1% chance of a slip and two emails trashed; repeat the rule twice in the prompt
No real risk, since a model always obeys its Instructions; no change is needed
About an 87% chance of a slip and about 114 emails trashed; set the delete tool to Blocked
About a 50% chance of a slip; lower the temperature to zero so the rule holds
questions.explanation: With a 1% slip per action, the chance of at least one slip in 200 actions is 1 − 0.99^200 ≈ 87%, and the deck's expected number of emails trashed before you look is about 114. With the rule in the harness (the delete tool set to Blocked, or no connector that can delete), the expected damage is 0, with 200 proposed deletions to review. 'Put the rule where nothing the agent reads can reach it.' (The 1% is invented for teaching.)
questions.trap: A. 'Repeat the rule in the prompt' keeps the rule as a sentence the model reads; the next mail it reads can contradict it.
questions.tip: Prompt rule = a request (87% / about 114). Harness rule = a wall (0 / 200 to review). In Part B, name the setting, not the sentence.
questions.source: Where we met it: Week 6 lecture, the wall (prompt vs harness worked numbers)

questions.stem: A team builds a cloud routine that reads new Disqus comments at 3 AM and opens a pull request with its findings. A teammate says, 'It will ask us before it does anything risky.' Which statement is correct?
options: In the cloud nobody is asked; its wall is the connectors included and the pull request
It emails each risky call to the team, who approve it in the morning
It pauses at the first risky call until someone opens the Claude app
Its wall is the line 'ask before risky actions' in its Instructions
questions.explanation: Week 6: 'In the cloud, nobody is asked. A cloud routine runs without prompts, so its wall is the connectors you include and what its environment reaches; a local one can still stop and wait for you.' Here the gate is that it can only open a pull request, and nothing merges until a person approves it. After the run, the team reads the record: what it read, what it called, where it stopped.
questions.trap: B. The Instructions line is tempting, but a sentence in the prompt only asks; a cloud routine never stops to ask anyone.
questions.tip: Cloud routine = no prompts, so untick every connector the job does not need. Local session = it can stop and wait at the permission dialog.
questions.source: Where we met it: Week 6 lecture, 'Where the person sits' and the wall; Week 8 AIS (cloud routines)

Define the five things an unattended agent needs, explain why memory and the stop rule must be built, write them for this case, and say where the manager stays in the loop.

questions.stem: Match each of Week 6's four levels to what the agent may do and who is exposed if it is wrong.

pairs.right: Reads and reports what is there: you, and only your time
Writes replies that a person sends: nobody outside, because you read the draft first
Asks before each send, then sends once you allow it: you and the recipient, once you click
Sends without asking: the recipient, your firm, and you afterwards

questions.explanation: 'The level decides who is exposed when it is wrong.' Choose the level by asking who gets hurt, not how clever the model is; keep the rule in the wall (send Blocked or Needs approval), not in the prompt.
questions.trap: Thinking Draft means the agent sends after you click. That is Act with approval.
questions.tip: Who presses send? You = Draft. The agent after you allow = Act with approval.
questions.source: Where we met it: Week 6 lecture, 'How much may the inbox agent do?'

questions.stem: A claims agent replies in plain text: 'Sure, I'll pay about four hundred on claim 88.' What does a well-built harness do with this?
options: Pays S$400, because the model's intention is clear from its sentence
Asks the model to guess the exact amount, then makes that payment
Sends the sentence to the customer as confirmation of the payment
Finds no valid tool call in the agreed format, runs nothing and returns an error
questions.explanation: A harness runs only a tool call written in the fixed format set in advance: a tool name and fields, usually JSON, such as pay_claim {"claim": 88, "amount": 400}. Before anything runs it checks that it can parse the text, that the tool exists and the fields are valid. A friendly sentence is not a call, so nothing runs.
questions.trap: A. 'The intention is clear' describes what a person would read into it. Software acts only on a valid call, which is exactly what keeps vague text from moving money.
questions.tip: Text becomes an action only when the harness can parse a valid tool call and its rules allow it.
questions.source: Where we met it: Week 7 lecture (Building AI Agents I), how text becomes an action

questions.stem: A credit agent's written reasoning says the borrower's repayment cover is '12 times', well above the bank's 1.25 minimum. Before signing the loan, what should the reviewer check?
options: The reasoning text again, since it explains each step in full
Whether two other agents reach the same '12 times' answer
Whether the model is the newest version on the market
The run record: what each tool returned and where each figure came from
questions.explanation: In the Week 7 case the record showed get_accounts had returned the 2023 accounts and get_loan returned 50,000 per month, so yearly repayments were 600,000 and the real cover was 1.0, below the 1.25 minimum. 'The reasoning read well. Only the record showed the two numbers it used.' Reasoning is more generated text; the record shows what actually happened.
questions.trap: A. Asking other agents feels like independent checking, but agreement is the weakest evidence: several agents can be confidently wrong together.
questions.tip: When an agent's reasoning and its record could differ, trust the record: the tool calls and their results.
questions.source: Where we met it: Week 7 lecture, the credit-memo record example

questions.stem: A bank uses AI to check each small-business loan file against its lending rules (income ratios, documents present). A named credit officer must approve every loan, because the bank answers for each decision and the AI cannot tell whether documents are genuine. Where does this task sit on the Week 7 Map of Human-AI Collaboration?
options: Right answer + either can work alone: AI alone, with checks
Right answer + must work together: A person leads, AI inside
No single right answer + must work together: Agents run it, a person judges
No single right answer + either can work alone: A person decides, AI alongside
questions.explanation: The map asks two questions of each task. Is there a right answer? Yes: each rule is met or not. Must people and AI do it together? Yes: the bank answers for each decision, the officer must approve every file, and the AI cannot judge whether documents are genuine. That is the top-left quadrant, 'A person leads, AI inside', where the person signs off what the agent has checked. The course's example for this quadrant is a loan file.
questions.trap: A. 'AI alone, with checks' is tempting because the rules are exact. But spot checks suit routine work; here a person must sign each decision.
questions.tip: Rules + a person who must sign every case = top-left 'A person leads, AI inside'. Rules + spot checks on routine cases = bottom-left 'AI alone, with checks'.
questions.source: Where we met it: Week 7, The Map of Human-AI Collaboration, slides 3 to 5; Group 4's Expense Claim Pre-Check (Week 8)

questions.stem: For Problem Set 5 a student shows a screenshot of the email her Zap sent. The brief asks for the Zap history exported as JSON. Why is the screenshot not enough?
options: Zap history is Zapier's own record of each run, with the data in and out
A screenshot is too large a file to upload to eLearn with the brief
The JSON lets the grader re-run the Zap from their own account
Zap history shows the prompt the model received at every step
questions.explanation: Zap history is 'the record Zapier itself keeps of every run of your Zap, so it shows that your Zap really ran'. A screenshot shows that an email arrived, not that the run happened as described. questions.source: Where we met it: Problem Set 5 brief; Week 7 Zapier AIS; Group 4 (Week 8)

questions.stem: A Zapier agent drafts replies to customer complaints. Line 4 of its Problem Set 5 agent card reads 'It must never: send a reply to a customer.' What must complete that line?
options: A second sentence in the AI step's prompt: 'Do not send anything.'
A note that the manager will read the Zap history once a month
The setting that stops it: the Gmail step is Create Draft, not Send Email
A statement that the model was tested on 100 earlier complaints
questions.explanation: The card's line is 'It must never: [ONE THING, AND THE SETTING THAT STOPS IT]'. A setting is something the harness enforces; a prompt can only ask. With Create Draft as the Gmail step, the Zap has no sending action at all, so no sentence anywhere can make it send. Group 4's feedback assistant used exactly this setting.
questions.trap: A. The extra prompt sentence feels like a second lock, but it is still a request the model reads.
questions.tip: Every 'never' rule in an answer needs the setting that enforces it: Create Draft, a fixed To field, a blocked tool, a connector left out.
questions.source: Where we met it: Problem Set 5 agent card; Group 4's MBairline Feedback Assistant (Week 8)
